> # The ftr feature-tree documentation system
> 
> Repo: `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr`. The machinery is 5 Python scripts + 1 HTML page + 1 vite plugin + 1 skill + 1 hook, driving a 1620-file markdown tree.
> 
> ## 1. The feature tree format
> 
> **Location and shape.** `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/features/ftr/**`. Every node is a *folder*; the folder contains `&lt;leafname&gt;.md` plus child folders. Depth runs to 12 path segments; 988 nodes carry code refs, 1150 classified requests are recorded. The governing spec is `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/.claude/skills/feature-tree/SKILL.md` (the format invariants section).
> 
> **Node anatomy** — no YAML frontmatter; conventions are HTML comments plus fixed headings:
> 
> 1. `# Title`
> 2. `*one-line purpose*`
> 3. optional `&lt;!-- deprecated-by: path --&gt;` + `**† deprecated** — superseded by [x](#path) *("evidence quote")*`, or `&lt;!-- status: not-used-yet --&gt;` / `not-implemented` marker (dims the whole subtree in the viewer)
> 4. `&lt;!-- ctx session=&lt;8-char&gt; ts=&lt;exact ISO ts&gt; --&gt;` — the anchor that links the node back to the precise conversation turn
> 5. the **verbatim** user prompt as a blockquote, labelled `**first request**` / `**refinement**` / `**bugfix**` (or `&gt; *(no single founding prompt — this node groups its sub-features)*` for structural nodes)
> 6. optional `## rule` — one present-tense testable requirement, written when the prompt was a complaint with no stated requirement (177 nodes have one)
> 7. `## implementation` — agent-written prose citing code as `` `path/file.ts:120-145` ``
> 
> Representative node, `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/features/ftr/haze/stability/gpu-lockup/gpu-lockup.md`:
> 
> ```markdown
> # WebGPU demo machine lockup
> *The webGPU demo locked up the whole machine; must not hang the system.*
> 
> &lt;!-- ctx session=cc232d60 ts=2026-07-05T01:04:11.094Z --&gt;
> &gt; **bugfix** — 2026-07-05, session `cc232d60`
> &gt;
> &gt; ok, we may have lost a little work because the machine totally locked up...
> 
> ## rule
> At most one WebGPU context is live on this machine at a time. A tool that opens the app opens its
> own browser and quits it on every exit path...
> 
> ## implementation
> No engine code changed. ... `scripts/appcheck.py:13-21`, `240-262` ... registers `close_browser`
> with `atexit` rather than a `try`/`finally` ... (`scripts/appcheck.py:108-121`).
> ```
> 
> **Mapping request → rules → notes → code** is therefore: prompt (verbatim, immutable) → `## rule` (derived requirement) → `## implementation` prose → backticked `file:line-range` refs, which the indexer turns into the reverse (code→feature) direction. Cross-node links use hash routing: `[pre](#ftr/loop/engine/looping/pre)`.
> 
> **Sibling ordering** is a separate dotfile `.order.md` per parent with ≥2 children, e.g. `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/features/ftr/.order.md`:
> 
> ```markdown
> # guide order
> 1. haze — the GPU renderer is the foundation everything else is drawn with
> 2. loop — the DJ system (analysis, playback, booth) is built on top of haze
> ...
> ```
> Parsed identically by `feature_viewer.py` and `features-routes.ts`; unlisted children trail alphabetically.
> 
> **Editorial rules** (SKILL.md `## Implementation sections`) are unusually strict and clearly enforced in the prose: insight not facts, define a term at the least common ancestor, never restate an ancestor, no "burble" (explicit banned-phrase list), honesty beats coverage ("if a request was never built, say so"). There is also an "iteration journeys" convention: a burst of one-line refinements keeps one node per request, and the *parent* closes with a `**The journey:**` paragraph telling the arc.
> 
> **Fan-out limit**: 4 children ideal, 6 hard; over that, a grouping pass invents structural nodes and `git mv`s subtrees, then rewrites paths in `requests.jsonl` / `deprecations.json` (ctx anchors are path-independent and survive).
> 
> ## 2. The pipeline
> 
> **Mining** — `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/feature_extract.py` (75 lines). Walks `~/.claude/projects/-Users-asnaroo-Desktop-ftr/*.jsonl` sorted by session start time, keeps only `type == "user"`, non-`isMeta` turns whose content is real text, and drops tool results (`&lt;`-prefixed), `Caveat:`, `[Request interrupted`, continuation summaries, and trivial acks via a length+charset heuristic:
> 
> ```python
> if len(text) &lt; 25 and len(text.split()) &lt;= 4 and re.fullmatch(r"[\w\s!\.\-:\)\(\?…'’\",]*", text):
>     continue  # trivial ack ("go !", "yes do that", ...)
> ```
> Emits `{id, session, ts, text}` JSONL; `--since`/`--id-base` make it incremental against the watermark.
> 
> **Classification is not code** — it is a model following SKILL.md step 2 (`skip` | `feature` | `refinement` | `bugfix`, plus tree path/title/purpose), subagents if &gt;~100 requests. Roughly 1/3 of extracted prompts get skipped. Current split in `requests.jsonl`: 605 refinements, 305 features, 240 bugfixes.
> 
> **Incremental state**: `features/.state.json` = `{"last_ts": "2026-08-11T21:37:29.333Z", "max_id": 1825, "n_requests": 1150}`. `features/.index/requests.jsonl` is append-only; `features/.index/deprecations.json` holds high-confidence supersession pairs with verbatim evidence quotes and a `confidence` field.
> 
> **The 9-step update procedure** (SKILL.md `## Update procedure`): extract → classify → insert nodes + update `.order.md` + grouping pass → deprecation sweep → write implementation sections → `feature_query.py --stale --fix` then `--index` → persist state → `feature_convo.py` mirror → report. Step 6 is emphatic: "a tree with unrepaired CHANGED refs is misinformation."
> 
> **The hook** — `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/feature_hook.py`, wired in `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/.claude/settings.json` as a `PreToolUse` hook matching `Edit|Write` (10 s timeout, statusMessage "Checking the feature tree"). It reads the payload's `tool_input.file_path`, relativises it, looks it up in `refs.json`, dedups by node keeping the widest range, caps at 8 nodes, and returns `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` with `suppressOutput: true` — so intent lands in context *before* the edit. Notable details: it skips files under `features/` and outside the repo, dedups once-per-file-per-session via `/tmp/ftr-feature-hook-&lt;session_id&gt;.txt`, annotates nodes that have a `## rule`, and logs to `features/.index/usage.jsonl`. Quiet by design: no refs → no output.
> 
> **Log mirroring** — `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/feature_convo.py` copies the `~/.claude` logs *whole* (~365 MB, gitignored at `.gitignore:23`) into `features/.index/logs/`, so the deployed viewer's conversation pane works on the Mac mini. Incremental by mtime. Credential shapes are redacted on the way out (`sk-ant-…`, `ghp_…`, `AKIA…`, `xox[baprs]-…`, PEM headers, plus a `key: value` form), with replacements chosen to keep the JSON line valid. `--check` is a dry run. `scripts/deploy.sh:39` runs it on every release.
> 
> ## 3. feature_query.py
> 
> `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/feature_query.py` (318 lines). It is the code→feature direction.
> 
> - `--index` walks every `&lt;leaf&gt;.md` and regex-extracts backticked refs (`REF_RE` over extensions ts|tsx|js|rs|py|wgsl|html|json|toml|sh|md|css), storing per ref: `node`, `title`, `file`, `from`, `to`, a whitespace-normalised sha1 `hash` of the cited lines, and an `anchor` (first non-blank cited line, 160 chars). Output `features/.index/refs.json` with a `baseline` = current git HEAD. Currently **3597 refs across 144 files and 988 nodes**, all `state: ok`. Partial refs (`stages/grid.py`) resolve by unique suffix match over a repo file map.
> - `--for-file src/playback.ts:719` (or bare path) — every node whose ref range covers the line, sorted by each node's *founding request timestamp* (read back out of the `ctx` comment), so history reads oldest-first.
> - `--find stem mute` — intent→code: nodes whose path + purpose + ref titles contain all terms, printed with their code ranges (or "(no code refs)").
> - `--rules` — dumps every `## rule` section, i.e. the machine-readable spec (177 of them).
> - `--never-built` — regex over implementation bodies for `never built|no code exists|was not implemented|does not exist in the repo|not implemented`, printing ±90 chars of context. Deliberately a prose convention, not structured data.
> - `--deprecated` — nodes with a `deprecated-by:` marker and their successor.
> - `--stale [--fix]` — the three-way honesty check: hash matches → ok; hash differs but the anchor is found exactly once elsewhere and the range re-hashes → **DRIFT**, and `--fix` rewrites the backticked ref in the md then reindexes; anchor gone → **CHANGED**, and it names the commit (`git log --oneline -1 baseline..HEAD -- file`) so prose can be re-read.
> 
> Every invocation appends to `features/.index/usage.jsonl` (`{ts, via: "cli", args}`), so consultation rate is measurable — 126 entries so far, mixed `hook` and `cli`.
> 
> ## 4. The viewer
> 
> Two servers, one page. `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/feature_viewer.py` (local, stdlib `ThreadingHTTPServer` on 127.0.0.1:5178, reading `~/.claude` directly) and `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/features-routes.ts` (a vite plugin serving `/features/` on the deployed site, reading the mirrored logs). Both expose the same endpoints — `/tree`, `/md`, `/code`, `/refs`, `/anchors`, `/convo` — and both serve `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/feature_viewer.html`, whose fetches are base-relative so one page works at `/` and at `/features/`.
> 
> Three panes:
> - **Tree** — built by `build_tree`, carrying per node: `.order.md` order, `deprecated`, `status`, `ts`, and `upd` (newest ts in the subtree). Sort modes `guide | newest first | oldest first | a-z`, persisted in `localStorage.ftrSort`. Deprecated/status subtrees are dimmed with a chip.
> - **Markdown** — rendered with `marked` from a CDN, plus post-processing: `wireCodeRefs` turns any `&lt;code&gt;` matching `file.ext:120-145` into a click-to-expand inline snippet fetched from `/code` (clamped to 80 lines), with an "open" link and **backlink chips** from `/refs` listing the *other* features citing those same lines, each navigating the tree. `#ftr/...` links go through a hashchange router.
> - **Conversation** — clicking a request opens the original session log scrolled to the exact turn (`markAnchor` finds the first turn with `ts &gt;= anchor`). `build_anchors` maps `session|ts` → node, making it two-way: a turn in the transcript that founded a feature is clickable back to its node. Missing log → "no log found for session …". The pane follows but never self-opens.
> 
> Security posture of `/code`: it will serve an 80-line excerpt of *any* file resolvable inside the repo, and the path check is a `startsWith(REPO)` realpath guard.

> ## 5. scripts/auth-gate.ts — the login technique
> 
> `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr/scripts/auth-gate.ts` (379 lines) is a **passwordless SMS one-time-PIN gate**, described as "a port of the nøøb muon login flow", implemented as a vite middleware plugin that must be registered first.
> 
> - **Selective gating**: only tunnel traffic is gated. `const fromTunnel = (req) =&gt; !!req.headers["cf-connecting-ip"]` — cloudflared always stamps it, so the local rig on the LAN stays frictionless.
> - **Flow**: phone number → invite check against `~/.ftr-auth/users.json` (`[{name, phone}]`; names starting with `_` are test users whose PIN is console-logged, not texted) → 4-digit PIN via **Vonage** (`https://rest.nexmo.com/sms/json`, creds from `~/.agent-config.json` or env) → cookie.
> - **Token**: not a JWT. `payload = "&lt;digits&gt;.&lt;expiry&gt;"`, cookie value `payload.HMAC-SHA256(payload, secret)`, verified with `timingSafeEqual`; 365-day session. The secret is a 32-byte random hex in `~/.ftr-auth/secret` (mode 0600), auto-generated on first use.
> - **State deliberately outside the repo** in `~/.ftr-auth/` so `rsync --delete` on deploy can't wipe the invite list. Pending PINs are persisted to `pending.json` (mode 0600) because vite restarts on config reload and an in-memory map orphaned already-texted codes.
> - **Limits**: 5-minute PIN TTL, 3 attempts, 5 SMS/hour per phone.
> - **Extras**: `sessionOf(req)` derives a filename-safe per-user session name (all local traffic shares `"local"`); `wsAuthed` gates the WS relay; the login page is stamped with the git short SHA to defeat cache confusion; responses use `no-store, must-revalidate` because Safari reused a cached 401.
> - **Relevant to the tree**: `/features` and everything under it is explicitly allowlisted past the gate — "the feature tree is deliberately public — a shareable artefact, no login needed", with the code's own honest caveat: *"Note this includes /features/code, which serves excerpts of any repo file."*
> 
> ## 6. Honest assessment
> 
> **What works well**
> - The core invariant — one request, one node, verbatim, immutable — is what makes the artefact trustworthy. It cannot drift into a rewritten-history design doc, because refinements must become child folders.
> - The three-way staleness model (hash / anchor-relocate / genuine change) is the strongest piece of engineering here. It solves the real problem (line-number drift swamping real divergence) cheaply, and `--fix` makes maintenance nearly free. Current state is 3597/3597 `ok`.
> - Push, not pull: the PreToolUse hook puts intent in front of the agent at the moment of editing, with once-per-file-per-session dedup so it doesn't become noise. Plus `CLAUDE.md` instructs consulting the tree by default.
> - Self-instrumenting: `usage.jsonl` logs every consultation, and the design node `features/ftr/dev/workflow/feature-modular-spec/agent-integration/agent-integration.md` names the intended effect metric (re-break rate / repeat bugfix nodes per area, derivable from `requests.jsonl`).
> - The negative knowledge is the real payoff and is explicitly designed for: rejected approaches, `--never-built`, `--deprecated` with evidence quotes — none of it recoverable by reading code.
> - Two server implementations (Python and TS) share one HTML page, and the base-relative fetch trick keeps them honest.
> 
> **What is fragile or manual**
> - **The log path is hardcoded and currently wrong.** `feature_extract.py:14`, `feature_convo.py:26` and `feature_viewer.py:12` all point at `~/.claude/projects/-Users-asnaroo-Desktop-ftr`. The repo now lives at `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/ftr`, and Claude Code is writing new sessions to `~/.claude/projects/-Users-asnaroo-Desktop-experiments-ftr` (2 entries, newest today) while the mined dir's newest log is Aug 11. Any session since the move is invisible to extraction *and* to the conversation pane. There is also a stray third dir, `-Users-asnaroo-Desktop-ftr-features`. Nothing detects this — extract just reports "0 requests".
> - **Classification, insertion, grouping, deprecation sweep and implementation prose are all model judgement**, not code. The whole quality of the tree rests on an agent faithfully executing a ~250-line skill file. Cost scales with request volume, and the tree is only as current as the last time someone said "update the feature tree".
> - **Refs are hand-written into prose.** The index only reads what an agent typed; a wrong-but-plausible range indexes cleanly as `ok`. Accuracy is asserted, never derived.
> - **Sessions are keyed by an 8-char filename prefix** — collision-prone in principle, and a deleted log silently kills every ctx anchor in it (SKILL.md accepts this: "the viewer shows 'no log found', which is acceptable").
> - `--never-built` is a **regex over English prose** (`never built|not implemented|…`), so it is only as good as the phrasing convention; it will both miss and false-positive.
> - The `refs.json` `baseline` is a stale commit (`a3fd53c`, 3 commits behind HEAD `1a382d7`), so `--stale`'s "which commit changed it" reporting and touched-file count are already drifting — a reminder that step 6 is manual.
> - The ack filter in `feature_extract.py:54` is a crude length+charset heuristic; a short but substantive instruction gets dropped silently.
> - The grouping pass rewrites paths across `requests.jsonl`, `deprecations.json`, `deprecated-by:` markers and `.order.md` files — a multi-file consistency edit with no verification tool. Nothing checks that a `deprecated-by:` target still exists.
> - Ordering data lives in `.order.md` prose files that nothing validates against the child set; SKILL.md admits "a child missing from `.order.md` still renders — it trails alphabetically".
> - `/features/code` is public-by-design and will excerpt any repo file. The redaction in `feature_convo.py` is regex-shaped credential matching over ~365 MB of raw transcript — best-effort, not a guarantee, and the logs contain full tool output and file contents.
> - 14 nodes still carry the `*(to be written)*` stub implementation, and SKILL.md's own caveat notes implementation sections are a separate pass that must never be overwritten — an ordering constraint enforced only by instruction.
> 
> **Known limitations stated in the code/docs**: SKILL.md `## Caveats` (dead anchors from deleted logs; implementation sections written by a separate pass and never overwritten; `.index/` and `.state.json` committed deliberately), the auth-gate's own note about `/features/code`, `features-routes.ts`'s note that a fresh clone sees "no log found", and the fan-out/grouping section's admission that regrouping is "judgement calls, not mechanical bisection".</result>

> # microserver.fm — architectural summary
> 
> Repo: `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/microserver.fm` (last commit Jul 2024, `79533db tweak`). ~1400 lines of hand-written source; the rest is generated JS and journal.
> 
> ## 1. Layout and documents

> | `/source/ts/util/fnf.ts` (392) | The **literate build tool**: markdown → `.fm.ts` transpiler + source-mapper + `tsc` driver + test runner. Written as plain TS (deliberately non-fm, see below). |

> 
> ## 2. The core mechanism
> 
> A feature is a **class whose name starts with `_`, decorated `@feature`, extending its parent feature** (not a base class — inheritance edges *are* the feature tree). Methods inside carry `@def | @replace | @before | @after | @on`. Nothing is called as a method; every method is *poked into module/global scope as a free function*, so call sites are plain `hello("world")`.
> 
> Registration (`fm.ts:154-211`) — every decorator does the same thing, differing only in a string tag:
> 
> ```ts
> export function feature&lt;T extends {new(...a:any[]):{}}&gt;(constructor: T) {
>     const className = constructor.name;                 // e.g. "_Get"
>     const superClassName = Object.getPrototypeOf(constructor.prototype).constructor.name;
>     if (!className.startsWith("_")) throw new Error(...);
>     const mf = MetaFeature._findOrCreate(className);
>     mf.initialise(superClassName, new constructor() as _Feature);  // singleton instance
>     fm.buildFeature(mf);                                // compose immediately, in load order
> }
> export function after(target:any, key:string, d:PropertyDescriptor) {
>     MetaFeature._findOrCreate(target.constructor.name)
>         .addFunction(new MetaFunction(key, d.value, "after"));
> }
> ```
> 
> Composition (`fm.ts:397-508`) — the whole trick. `functionRegistry` shadows a `Proxy` over `globalThis`; each build *wraps whatever function currently has that name*:
> 
> ```ts
> buildFeature(mf: MetaFeature) {
>     for (const mfn of mf.functions) {
>         let newFunction = this.buildFunction(mf, mfn);          // def/replace/on/after/before
>         Object.defineProperty(newFunction, "name", { value: mfn.name });
>         if (this.isDebugging &amp;&amp; mf.logging) newFunction = this.logFunction(mf, mfn, newFunction);
>         this.replaceModuleScopeFunction(mfn.name, newFunction);  // poke into global scope
>     }
> }
> buildAfterFunction(mf, mfn) {                 // the representative combinator
>     const originalFunction = functionRegistry[mfn.name];
>     if (!originalFunction) throw new Error(`${mf.name}.after: '${mfn.name}' not found`);
>     return function (...args:any[]) {
>         let _result = originalFunction(...args);
>         return mfn.method.apply(mf.instance, [...args, _result]);   // prior result appended as extra arg
>     };
> }
> ```
> 
> Semantics worth carrying forward:
> - `@def` defines (throws if the name exists); `@replace` overrides and can reach the prior definition via `this.existing(fn)` (which resolves fn→name via a `Map&lt;Function,string&gt;` and looks up `MetaFeature.existing[name]`).
> - `@before` runs first and **short-circuits**: if it returns anything other than `undefined`, the original never runs. This is the dispatch mechanism the server is built on — `_Get` and `_Put` each `@before handle_request`.
> - `@after` receives the original's return value appended to the arg list.
> - `@on` runs the new function *in parallel* with the old via `Promise.all`; requires async, unchecked at compile time (readme calls this "a bit dangerous… c'est la guerre").
> - Runtime reconfiguration: `fm.disable(["_Hello"])` flips `enabled` flags then `rebuild()` — clear all globals and re-run `buildFeature` over `MetaFeature._all` in declaration order. This means **feature ordering = source load order**, and enabling/disabling is a full re-link. `fm.debug(true)` re-links with logging wrappers.
> - Data: features are function-only. State is `@struct` classes + `make(Colour,{r:1})` for named/defaulted construction, extended later by a *second* class `@extend(Colour)` that chains into a global `_initialisers[name]` — plus a hand-written `interface Colour { a: number }` merge so TS type-checks. Structural extension is thus half-automatic and needs the duplicate interface declaration.
> - Every function needs a hand-written `declare const foo: (…) =&gt; …;` at module scope so TS accepts the free-function call sites. `fnf.ts` exists partly to generate these.
> - Logging is deeply woven in: `Log`/`LogLine` trees, an async-context hack (`tagged_function` names a wrapper `__asynclog__N` and finds it by **parsing `new Error().stack`**) so async subtrees nest correctly, and RPC responses ship `{result, log}` so a server-side log tree is spliced into the client's log (`shared.fm.ts:79-84`). This is the most inventive and most fragile part.
> 
> ## 3. The literate angle
> 
> `fnf` = **feature normal form**. `source/fnf/*.fnf.md` is markdown where **4-space-indented lines are code** and prose is everything else; `fnf.ts` (`convertMarkdownToCode`, lines 150-212) does:
> 
> - indented lines → code; lines containing `==&gt;` become **tests**: `x ==&gt;` → `fm._output(await x, line)`, `x ==&gt; y` → `fm._assert(await x, y, line)`. Collected into an `async _test()` method injected into the feature class.
> - keyword-at-line-start rewriting: `feature X extends Y;` → `@feature export class _X extends _Y {` (auto-underscoring and auto-closing the brace), and `def/on/replace/after/before/struct/extend` → the corresponding `@decorator`.
> - auto-generates `declare const` lines by regexing `@def` signatures into a persistent `declarations.d.ts`, then scanning the body for called names (`findFunctions`).
> - emits `//@ &lt;mdline&gt;` markers per line, strips them into `build/fnf/sourceMap.json`, and rewrites `tsc` error output back into `file.md(line,col)` (`processBuildLog`). Genuine literate-programming ergonomics.
> - generates `source/ts/import/all.ts` ordering feature imports **by file creation date** — the feature tree's build order is the filesystem birthtime. Fragile, and clearly a placeholder.
> 
> The successor of this idea lives in the sibling `/Users/asnaroo/Desktop/experiments/fnf` (Sep 2024): same literate markdown, but `.fnf.&lt;lang&gt;.md`, implemented in Python, multi-backend (`languages/typescript.py`, `backends/deno.py`), with `local` variables, `struct`, `&gt; expr ==&gt; value` console lines, and an explicit LLM-translation agenda in its readme.

> 
> The server (`server.fm.ts`) is four features stacked by `@before` on one chain:
> 
> - `_Server`: `os.serve(receive_request, {port: 8000})`; `handle_request` → `not_found()` (404).
> - `_Get`: `@before handle_request` intercepts `GET` → `serve_file`; `translate_path` maps `/` → `/index.html` under `public/`; hand-rolled `mime_type` switch (5 types).
> - `_GetJS`: `@replace translate_path` calling `this.existing(...)` to redirect `.js`/`.js.map` to `build/js`. This is the readme's canonical override pattern in production use.
> - `_Put`: **RPC as a feature.** `PUT /functionName` with a JSON body → `fm.getModuleScopeFunction(name)` → call with `Object.values(params)` → respond `{result, log}`. Note there is **no allow-list, no auth, no origin check** — any module-scope function is callable by name. Fine for localhost, unshippable otherwise.
> - Client side (`shared.fm.ts` `_Device.remote`) wraps a *local* function in a `Proxy` whose `apply` maps positional args to names using `fm.getFunctionParams(name)` and does the fetch, so `await remote(server, greet)("asnaroo")` looks like a local call. Elegant; the design's real payoff.

In microserver.fm this was never implemented — it exists only as **design sketches in `scribbles.md:76-140` and `173-205`**, which are the most valuable pages for a successor:

> ```ts

> The stated rule: a function touching a shared/server variable is *server-tagged*; one touching the DOM is *client-tagged*; anything else is "uncommitted" and may run either side; the compiler inserts `remote()` calls so **execution ping-pongs across the boundary** — all over `fetch`, no websockets. The author's conclusion (line 166): "roles need to become first-class citizens of the language", with `client:` / `server:` / `anywhere:` sections *inside one feature clause* so both halves of an interaction are read together.

Both explorers are back. Let me save the key project context to memory, then give you the synthesis.

Here's the full picture from both codebases, and where I think it points.

## What each experiment proved

**microserver.fm (2024) — fm as code architecture.** The core mechanism is a `@feature` class (name starts with `_`, extends its parent feature — the inheritance tree *is* the feature tree) whose methods carry one of five combinators: `@def`, `@replace` (with `this.existing()` to reach the prior definition), `@before` (short-circuits — this is how `_Get`/`_Put` dispatch requests), `@after` (gets the prior result as an extra arg), and `@on` (parallel). Composition happens at load time by poking wrapped functions into global scope, so call sites are plain `hello("world")`. Runtime `fm.disable([...])` + full re-link demonstrably works, as do structs with `@extend`, the literate `fnf` markdown→TS pipeline with *reverse source maps* (compile errors report `.md` line numbers), and the `remote(server, greet)("asnaroo")` RPC proxy with server log trees spliced into the client's.

The decisive part: **your own verdict at the top of `scribbles.md`** — the global-scope poking is untenable (namespace clashes with node builtins, no way to namespace), so "generate proper typescript code… START A NEW PROJECT." Two other conclusions you reached and never built: roles (`client:` / `server:` / `anywhere:` sections inside one feature, with the compiler inserting `remote()` so execution ping-pongs across the boundary), and explicit feature ordering (it's currently *file creation date*, via the generated import list).

**ftr (2026) — fm as knowledge architecture.** Every user request becomes exactly one immutable node in `features/`: verbatim prompt with a `ctx` anchor into the actual conversation log, an optional derived `## rule` (177 of them — a testable spec), and agent-written `## implementation` prose citing `file:line` refs. The machinery around it is genuinely strong: 3597 refs kept honest by a three-way staleness check (hash-match / anchor-relocated-so-auto-fix / genuinely-changed-so-reread), a PreToolUse hook that pushes relevant intent into the agent's context *at the moment it edits a file*, `--never-built` and `--deprecated` capturing the negative knowledge no code reading can recover, and a viewer where a feature node links to the exact conversational turn that founded it, and back.

Its weaknesses are the mirror image of its strengths: classification, insertion, grouping, and implementation prose are all model judgement executing a skill file; code refs are hand-typed prose (asserted, never derived); and the update is manual — the tree is only as current as the last "update the feature tree". (Also a practical bug: the hardcoded log paths still point at the old repo location, so post-move sessions are invisible.)

## The unification thesis

The two experiments are the same idea attacked from opposite ends, and each has exactly what the other lacks:

- microserver.fm had **structure without provenance** — features composed mechanically, but nothing recorded *why* a feature existed or what the user actually asked for.
- ftr has **provenance without structure** — every feature's intent, rules, and history are captured, but the code itself is a conventional monolith; features exist only as annotations pointing into it.

And the thing that changed between 2024 and 2026 is the missing third ingredient: **the agent**. In 2024 you needed a fragile runtime (Proxy over globalThis, stack-parsing, regexing `Function.toString()`) to do the weaving mechanically. In 2026, the ftr experiment shows agents can reliably maintain the intent↔code mapping — so fm2 can put the agent *in the toolchain*: the feature node becomes the unit that holds intent (verbatim request), spec (rules), and source (literate code), and a deterministic weaver — not runtime patching — generates the composed program, while the agent handles everything that needs judgement. That would finally make "the feature is the smallest shippable unit" real: a feature node would be a self-contained thing you could share, disable, or commission, exactly as `nøøb.md` envisions.

## Design questions before I sketch anything concrete

1. **Tree-as-source vs tree-as-mirror.** ftr's tree is a *mirror* mined after the fact. The bolder fm2 move is tree-as-*source*: the `features/` node contains the literate code, and the buildable program is generated from the tree (with reverse source maps, so errors point back at nodes). Do you want to go all the way there, or keep code primary with a tighter, automated mirror?

2. **Composition semantics.** Do the five combinators (`def/replace/before/after/on`) survive as the composition model, now applied by a *generator* into namespaced plain TS? And is ordering declared explicitly per feature (a `.order`-like file, or dependency declarations), replacing birthtime order?

3. **The driving application.** Your own manifesto says systems can't be designed in a vacuum. What's fm2's forcing app — the nøøb.org site itself rebuilt feature-modularly? Something new? (The site is a nice candidate: it needs the auth gate, hosting on the mini, and would dogfood the viewer as its public face.)

4. **Language/runtime.** microserver.fm was TS/Deno; the sibling `fnf` project went Python with pluggable language backends. Is fm2 committed to TS, and is multi-language a v1 goal or a someday?

5. **Roles.** First-class `client:/server:/anywhere:` with automatic `remote()` insertion is the thing you designed twice and never built. In scope for v1, or does fm2 start single-runtime?

My instinct, if you want it: tree-as-source, combinators kept but applied by a generator, TS-only v1, roles in v1 (it's the payoff that justifies the generator), and the nøøb.org site as the forcing app — with ftr's staleness/hook/viewer machinery generalized so it's project-agnostic from day one. But you've lived with these ideas for two years; tell me where your head is now.

> ## 0. Headline: what changed since the 2024 ancestor

> The 2024 microserver.fm you know (`@feature` classes, combinators poked into global scope, namespace clashes) has been replaced by a **compile-once / link-many build over literate markdown**. Nothing is poked into global scope any more, and nothing is inlined into anyone's source. The five things to carry forward:
> 
> 1. **Feature = folder + one `.fm.md` literate spec.** Code lives in fenced blocks inside prose; generated code goes to a sibling `imp/`. Python + TypeScript/JS today; the spec file is language-agnostic.
> 2. **Composition is by directive comment above a function**: `@after` / `@before` / `@replace` (live), plus `@extend` (types), `@var`, `@needs`. `@on` (concurrent) and `@in` (call-site) are designed but **hard build errors — "not yet supported"**.
> 3. **The namespace-clash problem was solved by `G`, a per-product flat linkage table** (GOT/PLT analogy, explicitly). A contribution stays a normal function in its own module; the build generates a dispatcher per host. Nothing is mutated in place.
> 4. **Product ≠ feature tree.** A product (`products/&lt;codename&gt;/`, animal codenames) owns no code; it is an ordered directive list (`include`/`exclude`/`fork`/`dynamic`/`static`/`default`) materialised into a symlink mirror. **A feature's `.fm.md` is byte-identical whichever product composes it** — this is the constitution.
> 5. **`_enabled` is the single security/capability primitive**: `_enabled = _in_tool ∧ _user_wants ∧ _allowed`, enforced at three gates (mount, binding, dispatch), all three live since 2026-07-02.

> The snapshot doc for a fresh agent, 2026-07-31. **"Post-promotion" = the day `dev` was merged to `main` and production stopped serving the canonical muon shell and started serving a *built product* (`bilby`) under gunicorn.** Before it, the G-dispatch/product model lived only on dev; after it, `www.nøøb.org` is a generated product mirror. The deep argument: fm models every contribution as **call-and-return**, so there is no "during" — `@on` and `@after` collapse for anything that mutates state and returns. Fire-and-forget animation doesn't rescue it. **`@on` becomes real only with a temporal substrate** (async host that awaits, or generators/streams) — the "streams for zero" direction. Intended future default: **`@on` means "no ordering dependency"; `@after`/`@before` get reserved for a declared happens-before edge** (dataflow/instruction-scheduling shape) — today's `@after`-by-default over-specifies order everywhere. Load-bearing rule: *"a mount that waits for its anchor is independent; one that assumes order isn't."*

> Implementation spec for replacing in-place `apply` with generated `G`. Directive→dispatch table; **seam taxonomy** (whole-function seam keyed by name; call-site seam keyed `(O, A)` → `G.O__A`); the ownership rule (**owner = first feature to declare a top-level name in `.order.md` DFS walk order**; owner's body is the seam's **base**); async propagation; and the gating rules including the exemptions — never gate `/context`'s own contributions, never gate the boot lifecycle hosts `setup, mount, register_routes, navigate, connect` (they fire before the per-user context binds and every `_enabled` is class-default `False`). Also: `G` injection at boot via `setattr(mod, "G", G)`; the G↔feature cycle is safe **only because seam calls happen inside function bodies** — top-level code must never call a host at import, asserted in extract. Terminology note: "weave" was later banned (see decisions 2026-07-03) and folded into `/build`.
> 
> ### wire-architecture.md (67 lines) — network layer, mostly BUILT
> Driven by a measured problem: the muon shell client-rendered everything — 76 files / 273KB raw / 57KB gz fetched `no-store` before any code ran; 3–8s remote. **"Network cost is proportional to what *exists*, not what's *enabled* — violating the fm thesis at the wire layer."** Three layers: (1) **per-tool chunks** via esbuild `--splitting`, with the crux being that **client `G` goes late-binding** — each tool chunk registers its modules (`G.bind({feature: module})`) and dispatchers skip unregistered members, "semantically identical to the existing `_enabled` gate, since an unloaded tool is a disabled tool" — DONE 2026-06-11; (2) **server-rendered content surfaces** (pages become curl-/LLM-readable, zero JS for first paint) — **PARKED**, the one big unbuilt piece; (3) **import-map content hashing** — DONE. Phase C hot-swap in chunk mode also DONE (8/8).
> 
> ### feature-management.md (66 lines) — the FMT and "the constitution"
> Stub prose, but strategically the most important note for fm2. In a feature-modular OS the kernel's job is **managing features**, so the **feature management tool (FMT) *is* the kernel**, not an app. Verbs over features: **call / construct / curate / publish / grant / adopt / inspect**. Self-hosting (the verbs are themselves features); **its surface is the agent** — you talk to your OS. The **four sovereignty guarantees**: no forced run (`_user_wants` is your inviolable AND-term), no forced update, **no rescinded grant** (a grant is a one-way *transfer*, not a revocable permission — "a provider-held allow-list is a leash"), full transparency + control. Plus the line that keeps it honest: **capability is transferable and irrevocable; resources are not** — so a shared feature must run on the adopter's own resources (bring-your-own-key, the `@needs key` model). Status 2026-05-25: building the first primitive, local `tool-call`, from `experiments/localmodel`'s two-stage router; `none` from the picker is the bridge to `tool-construct`.
> 
> ### glossary.md (286 lines) + the enforced glossary
> `agent-notes/glossary.md` is the **2026-05-29 harvest** (provenance); the reconciled ~90-term standard now lives at **`core/fm/glossary/glossary.md`** and its `## retired terms` section is **machine-read by the build validator — a retired term in any spec's prose fails the build**. First red run: 159 violations across 43 specs. Notable rulings: **"seam" → extension**, **"slot" → host**, **"weave"/"woven"/"wire in" → the build / composed / contribute**, **"orchestration host" → lifecycle host**, "first-declarer" → owner, "distance scoring" → closest-wins, "app" retired as a noun ("per-app" → per-tool). This ratchet is unusual and worth stealing: *a coinage isn't settled until it has a glossary line, and the build enforces it.*
> 
> ### decisions.md (626 lines) and journal.md (407 lines)
> `decisions.md` is newest-at-top (after an archived header describing the dead `fm_cons`/borrow world). The July 2026 entries are ops-heavy: the promotion, server-doctor's three-week restart loop (`localhost` resolving `::1` against IPv4-only servers → ~382 false failures/day → 9 orphaned processes → forced reboot), `FM_CONTEXTS_DIR` isolation, disk cleanup (9.2 GB of dead-watchdog debris). The design-bearing entries are 2026-07-02/03: **one instance per feature** (`main.boot` claims the canonical twin's `sys.modules` key — "fix at the loader, not the features"), **the dispatch gate going live at the HTTP boundary only** (in-process calls are trusted feature wiring), the glossary enforcement, and the weave retirement.
> 
> `agent-notes/journal.md` is the *design* journal (the real one — see §4) and contains the single best fm2 seed I found: **"every place fm hand-writes 'X changed → recompute the Y that depends on X' is a derived stream waiting for a language that can declare it."** `relayout` is specimen #1. Also: *"before wiring a contract between two features, check whether a shared lower primitive already reflects both"* — the static half of an interaction usually dissolves; only the change-over-time half needs a contract.
> 
> ### rebuild-plan.md (122 lines)
> The discipline used to land the product model on prod source: rebuild on prod's feature source so the only allowed diffs are **relocation** and **the build/runtime seam**, uniform across products; anything else is a deliberate functionality change. Measured baseline: **47 of 61 features relocated untouched**; the 13 that changed were triaged into park / seam / "make declarative". Two leaks were fixed *by making composition express them* rather than editing features: `default &lt;tool&gt;` became a manifest directive (killing `task.default_tool()`), and reader's no-task bail was fixed in context scoping. Structure: `core/fm/muon` + siblings `explorer`, `daylight`, `fieldnote`, plus generated `products/`. Two items still unticked (build-tool spec/imp sync, phase-2 cherry-picks) but largely superseded by later work.

> ## 2. core/ — fm, one, zero
> 
> `~/nøøb/core/core.md` gives the three-stage ladder, `.order.md` = `fm, zero, one`:
> 
> &gt; "The end-goal is `/one`, a feature-modular operating system, written in `/zero`, a feature-modular programming language." fm is "a collection of prompts and tools for writing feature-modular applications in **any existing programming language**… this is how we hone our fundamental understanding of how the rubber meets the feature-modular road."
> 
> - **`core/one/one.md`** — 12 lines. Aspirational only: a real-time distributed FMOS written in zero using miso; its purpose is the four FMT verbs (create / find / manage / exchange features). "Achieved when we can compile a product written completely in zero into a binary OS image… without any legacy toolchain."
> - **`core/zero/`** — `zero.md` plus `types/` (numeric) and `zeta/`. A language sketch, not an implementation: literate `.zero.md` features, abstract numeric types (`uint`/`int`/`float` sized by the compiler), enums and struct types, **"real-time streams as first-class objects"** and "feature modularity instead of object orientation" among the design goals. Essentially dormant; the handover lists zero under "deliberately deferred".
> - **`core/fm/`** — the live system. Tree: `fm.fm.md` (187 lines, the pattern doc), `build/`, `glossary/`, `muon/`, and the three tools `explorer/`, `daylight/`, `fieldnote/`.
> 
> ### How fm is implemented today
> **A Python build tool that parses literate markdown, emits per-feature `imp/` source, rewrites call sites, and generates a per-product dispatch table.** Not decorators, not a runtime metaclass, not a language. Regex/line-based, not AST-based (explicitly acknowledged: "the regex reality").
> 
> Pipeline, `core/fm/build/.order.md` = `compose, extract, extensions, instrument, bootstrap, compile, new`. From `build.fm.md`:
> 
> &gt; `build` is the top-level driver of the **products-only, G-dispatch** pipeline: a feature is never built on its own — it is composed into a *product*… The feature tree is compiled **once, in place** — `build_canonical` extracts, transforms, and compiles every feature into its canonical `imp/`, product-independent. The product step is then thin… This is the compile-once / link-many model: **a feature is the unit of compilation, a product the unit of linking.**
> 
> Entry point is products-only by design: `build("bilby")` works, `build("core/fm/muon")` **raises** — "there is no standalone feature build to drift away from what ships."
> 
> **The central mechanism, concretely** — generated `~/nøøb/products/bilby/_g/imp/g.py` (78 lines; also `g.ts`, `g.js`):
> 
> ```python
> # AUTO-GENERATED by /build — per-product G dispatch table (Python).
> # main injects the feature modules via bind({name: module}); each
> # dispatcher reaches them through _reg at call time (the linkage table).
> _reg = {}
> def bind(registry): _reg.update(registry)
> def _ctx(): return _reg["context"].ctx()
> 
> def body_class():
>     r = _reg["app"].body_class()
>     r = _reg["muon"].body_class()
>     if _ctx().gate._enabled: r = _reg["gate"].body_class()
>     return r
> 
> def note_captured(note):
>     r = _reg["capture"].note_captured(note)
>     if _ctx().transcribe._enabled: _reg["transcribe"].note_captured(note)
>     if _ctx().diarize._enabled:    _reg["diarize"].note_captured(note)
>     if _ctx().anonymise._enabled:  _reg["anonymise"].note_captured(note)
>     return r
> ```
> 
> That is the whole idea in nine lines: static features called bare, dynamic features gated on their runtime `_enabled`, base-passthrough for hosts with no contributors, and the whole composition **readable as an artifact** (the stated advantage over the old inlining `apply`). Only 9 slots in bilby — hosts are deliberately few. `register_routes` fans out to 20 features.
> 
> Extract's job, from `extract.fm.md`: re-extract every feature every build, no mtime gating, because *"the G-transform rewrites each `imp/` file in place — routing extension-point calls to `G.&lt;slot&gt;`, qualifying cross-feature direct calls, rewriting `@var` refs, adding `_use` imports — so a skipped feature's `imp/` is left holding the transform's output, not extract's clean source."* Cross-feature *direct* (non-host) calls resolve by a **closest-wins name resolver** and bind through `_use("name")`.
> 
> **Bootstrapping is handled by freezing, not self-hosting.** Build tools are `.fm.md`-canonical but never go through the pipeline; the loop is `ops/frozen-extract.sh &lt;tool&gt; --check` against `.frozen-build/`, and the done-test is `core/fm/build/round_trip_test.py` — **every build-tool spec must reproduce its `imp/*.py` byte-for-byte**, so doc and code cannot drift. Golden fixtures pin input→output.
> 
> ### `core/fm/fm.fm.md` — the pattern doc (read this one in full for fm2)
> Contains the `@after`/`@extend` worked examples, the mandated spec shape (`## introduction / interface / implementation / tests / demo`), and two sections worth lifting wholesale:
> - **authoring rules** the toolchain can't enforce: use the glossary; **one line per paragraph, never hard-wrap** (the reader reflows); a feature's source is stable across products; **don't name locals after features** (a real bug: `const reader = resp.body.getReader()` turned `linkifyFeatures(...)` into `reader.linkifyFeatures(...)`); a client mount must self-gate.
> - **capabilities and security**: `_enabled = _in_tool ∧ _user_wants ∧ _allowed`, `_status` ∈ `on / off_not_in_tool / off_user / needs_auth / needs_key` — *"`_status` is what turns a boolean into an experience"*; **a tool is a context that can require capabilities** ("daylight is logged-in-only" is not a feature inside daylight, it's the `@daylight` tool requiring auth); *"the server resolves; the server enforces"* — the client's copy of the context exists only to draw the right UI.
> 
> The `## demo` block is the other load-bearing invention: an interactive contract that runs **visually** via `play(feature)` and **headlessly** via `run_verify(feature, cid)` — the same script is documentation, regression test, and (proposed) the thing a cross-boundary reference pins to.
>

> ## 3. muon and products/bilby/muon
> 
> **muon is not a product — it's the runtime**, `core/fm/muon/muon.fm.md`: *"Where `/fm` is the build toolchain, `/muon` is the runtime that every fm product wants… the standard library you reach for the moment you build any product on `/fm`."* Language-scoped: today `/fm/muon`, later `/zero/muon`. 33 features in four buckets (`.order.md` = run, session, test, ui):
> 
> - `run` — `app` (Flask), `rpc` (RPC + SSE), `swap` (hot-swap), `resolve` (closest-wins name lookup), `linemap` (rewrite tracebacks back to `.fm.md` line numbers), `main` (product boot / `wsgi_app()`).
> - `session` — `login`, `context`, `private`, `debug`, `task`.
> - `test` — `demo` (+`sim`, `master`), `harness`, `snapshot` (+`calibrate`, `overlay`), `calllog`.
> - `ui` — `style`, `toolbar`, `reader` (+`markdown`, `collapsible`, `live-update`, `select`), `map`.
> 
> The **login flow** is `muon/session/login`: *"enter a name, receive a four-digit code by text message, type it in… once verified, the device is trusted until the user logs out"* (three tries, five minutes). The `/login` path exists as its own surface specifically so iOS Safari's SMS QuickType heuristic surfaces the incoming PIN.
> 
> Muon's discipline is the reusability rule you'll want in fm2: **muon contains no `@after` extensions *into* a product** — consumer-side extensions live in the tool's own subtree and contribute *up* into muon's hosts. "Muon never reaches back into a tool."
> 
> ### `products/bilby/` — the materialised manifest (and the `.hash.md` files)
> `products/&lt;codename&gt;/` is **generated and gitignored except the manifest**. `products/bilby/bilby.md` is the whole source of the product:
> 
> ```
> include muon
> dynamic explorer
> dynamic daylight
> dynamic fieldnote
> default explorer
> ```
> 
> with prose explaining the load-bearing choice: the three tools are `dynamic`, not `include`, because a `static` daylight contribution would fire on explorer pages too (`gate.body_class` returning `daylight-gated` everywhere).
> 
> `products/bilby/muon/` is the evaluated snapshot — **relative symlinks back to canonical**:
> ```
> .order.md   -&gt; ../../../core/fm/muon/.order.md
> common      -&gt; ../../../core/fm/muon/common
> imp         -&gt; ../../../core/fm/muon/imp
> muon.fm.md  -&gt; ../../../core/fm/muon/muon.fm.md
> run/ session/ test/ ui/     (real dirs, recursing the same pattern)
> ```
> plus `_g/imp/{g.py,g.ts,g.js}` and `_chunks/` (per-tool esbuild bundles + `manifest.json` of sha256[:10] hashes).
> 
> **`.hash.md` (62 of them in bilby) is the `name + hash` reference from composition-model.md, materialised.** One line, two fields:
> ```
> fccfaa8135c2  core/fm/muon
> b39d8419be88  core/fm/fieldnote
> 6664674fd4bc  core/fm/fieldnote/transcribe/diarize
> ```
> i.e. `&lt;subtree_hash&gt;  &lt;canonical path&gt;`. The subtree hash is over the feature's `.fm.md` + `.order.md` (imp excluded). It exists so the symlinks are a *regenerable cache*: `heal(product_dir)` re-resolves a dangling link by **name**, confirms the candidate by **hash**, and repoints — returning `{healed, broken}`, where `broken` is "moved *and* edited, won't guess." This is the resurrection of borrow's content fingerprint without borrow's copying.
> 
> Note the asymmetry vs. the design note: axolotl's manifest still documents `fork style` / `exclude map`, so fork and exclude are implemented; but bilby, the shipping product, uses none of them. Fork is built and effectively unexercised in production.

> **In flight / thin / unbuilt:**

The explorer has read the whole current repo — and it changes the picture substantially. Let me update my memory first, then give you the revised synthesis.

Full report is in from the mini, and I need to start by retracting most of my earlier synthesis: it was written against the 2024 ancestor, and the current fm has already built nearly everything I "proposed". Here's the corrected picture.

## What fm is now (July 2026, serving production)

The namespace-clash verdict was acted on long ago. Today's fm is a **compile-once / link-many build over literate markdown**: a feature is a folder with one `.fm.md` spec (code in fenced blocks, prose one-line-per-paragraph), extracted to a sibling `imp/`. Composition is `@after`/`@before`/`@replace` directives resolved into a **generated per-product flat dispatch table `G`** — the GOT/PLT analogy made literal, with static features called bare, dynamic ones gated on `_enabled`, and the whole composition readable as an artifact. A product (`bilby` = muon + explorer + daylight + fieldnote, live behind gunicorn on the mini) is nothing but a directive manifest (`include/exclude/fork/dynamic/static/default`) materialised into a symlink mirror with `name+hash` references that can `heal()`. `_enabled = _in_tool ∧ _user_wants ∧ _allowed` is the single capability primitive, enforced at three gates, with static-disabled features tree-shaken so clients can't even probe them. And the process discipline around it is remarkable: byte-exact round-trip tests for the build tools, done-tests proven red before green, and a **machine-enforced glossary** where using a retired term in any spec's prose fails the build.

**muon** is the runtime/stdlib (33 features — login, context, hot-swap, tracebacks mapped back to `.fm.md` lines, the `## demo` blocks that are simultaneously docs, regression tests, and proposed contract pins), with the discipline that muon never reaches back into a tool.

## The open holes the author left marked

These are explicit in the agent-notes, and they're where fm2's design space actually is:

1. **The temporal substrate.** `@on` and `@in` are deliberate hard build errors. `extension-semantics.md` argues fm's call-and-return model has no "during", so `@on` only becomes real with streams/async as a first-class substrate — and the intended inversion (`@on` = "no ordering dependency" as the *default*; `@after` reserved for declared happens-before edges) is the clearest flagged design change. `journal.md` has the seed: *"every place fm hand-writes 'X changed → recompute the Y that depends on X' is a derived stream waiting for a language that can declare it."* This is the on-ramp to zero.
2. **Type composition.** You can dispatch a call but not a struct field, so `@extend` on types is refused and composed types are per-product. Called "the unresolved hole at the centre of the model."
3. **Regex, not AST.** The whole toolchain is line/regex-based, acknowledged as the constraint blocking stronger guarantees (e.g. verifying `@on` independence rather than trusting the author).
4. **Source⇄derived recursion.** Directives → mirror → symlinks → `imp/` → chunks: five hand-built instances of "regenerable cache of the layer above," each with its own heal/rebuild/verify. fm2 could make that one first-class concept.
5. **The FMT.** The sovereignty constitution (feature management as the kernel, *the agent as its surface*, grants irrevocable, bring-your-own-resources) is prose only. Your own `.todo.md` points the same way: self-modifying agentic software, prompting in-app, edits with audit history that become reusable tool buttons.
6. Smaller: server-rendered content surfaces (parked), `fork` built but unexercised, zero/one deferred.

## Where ftr still fits

My unification thesis survives, but sharper now. Current fm has **spec without provenance**: `.fm.md` says what a feature *is*, but the verbatim request → rule → conversation-anchor chain lives only in hand-curated decisions.md/journal.md. ftr built exactly that missing layer — one immutable node per request, staleness-checked code refs, the PreToolUse hook, `--never-built`. And notice ftr's hook and fm's `_enabled` gates are the same shape: *intent enforced at the boundary, mechanically*. A successor could make provenance a per-feature concern — each feature carrying its own request history and rules inside the same folder as its `.fm.md` — rather than a parallel tree.

## So: what is fm2?

Given the nøøb repo is live production with its own momentum, and your experiments culture is "build with no fear of starting afresh," the real question is which frontier fm2 attacks. The candidates, as I see them:

- **A**: the **temporal substrate** — streams/derived-state as the composition default, unlocking `@on` and the `@after` inversion; effectively the first real step toward zero, prototyped in fm2.
- **B**: the **AST-based rebuild of the toolchain** — same semantics, real parsing, verifiable independence, and the source⇄derived recursion made generic (heal/rebuild/verify once, applied at every layer).
- **C**: the **provenance unification** — fold ftr's request-mining/staleness/hook machinery into the feature format itself, so a feature ships with its intent history; the FMT/agent-as-surface direction.

These aren't exclusive, but the first month's work differs a lot between them. Which itch is fm2 meant to scratch — and is there a forcing application in mind, or is the nøøb site itself (via a future product promotion) still the proving ground?

**The ring model is fm's capability model, generalized from code to data.** fm already has `_enabled = _in_tool ∧ _user_wants ∧ _allowed`, enforced server-side at three gates, with the sovereignty rule that a grant is a one-way transfer. Your promotion mechanism is exactly that shape applied to posts: visibility as capability, promotion as a quorum-agreed, irreversible-outward grant (you can't un-show something to a wider ring — which is *also* the honest GDPR framing, and "promotion is irreversible, so the default is private" is precisely the anti-blowback story). fm2's substrate could make one calculus serve both: which features you see and which posts you see are the same question, asked of the same context object. > - **A3** "The monolith's 170-line `/upload` (persist → thumbnail → geocode → transcribe → diarize → anonymise → report) inverts: `capture` emits `note_captured`; each stage `@on`s it. **The head of a pipeline must know nothing of its tail.**"
> - **A5** "Stamp intrinsic facts at write time; assign relationships post-hoc. Where a note *was* recorded (`locate`) is intrinsic; what it *belongs to* (`campaign`) is a relationship."
> - **A6** "Decomposition exposes conflations and bolt-ons. It revealed the monolith conflated *storage location* (per-campaign directories) with *membership* (a field) — separate them. It revealed `count` shares nothing with the app — drop it."
> - **A9** "Anything the target runtime already provides — the PWA/app shell, auth, rpc, the map widget — should factor *up*, never be reimplemented per tool. `shell` shrinks to app identity, auth becomes 'the tool `@needs auth`' plus the borrowed `/login`."

> **The "anatomy of a tool" framing — the single most useful thing for fm2's design:**
> 
> &gt; A tool's front door composes four standard surfaces: **see** (`ui/reader`), **act** (`ui/toolbar`), **ask** (`ui/command` — the agent surface, not yet shared), **move** (`ui/nav` — breadcrumb over the tool's object tree, not yet shared).
> &gt; "**Navigation is a breadcrumb over a tree, and that tree recurs at every scale of nøøb** — the feature tree (explorer), the campaign geography county → constituency → ward (fieldnote), the document corpus (daylight). Same surface, different tree."
> &gt; "**The anatomy is diagnostic — it shows a tool's *missing* surface.** explorer has all four; daylight lacks **move** (you can ask the corpus but not browse it); fieldnote lacks **ask** (you can record but not query the transcripts). > - **A8, the anti-abstraction rule, applied and then overruled:** `report.fm.md` — "The kinship with daylight's `/research` is noted but not merged: research is *agentic retrieval* over a vector index; this is *single-shot summary* of a small, fully-known corpus. Needs a retention clock (delete audio after transcription+anonymisation succeeds), encryption at rest, and lawful-basis/consent recording. Today consent is a social protocol ("holding the phone up to them like a microphone… so it was clear I was recording").

The political-app archaeology is back, and it's the most consequential report yet. Let me bank the durable facts, then give you the picture.

Here's what the deep dive into the three apps found — organized as what it means for fm2.

## The apps are realer than I expected — and the gaps are specific

**fieldnote was genuinely used in anger**: 3 users, 6 campaigns keyed to ONS ward codes, 110 clips / 1.1 GB across real canvassing bursts (March 31 – May 5, peaking 10 uploads/day around the locals), and the pipeline mostly ran — 76 of 80 notes transcribed, 68 anonymised, with street-level strategic reports that are recognizably the product working. **daylight** is a private alpha with 3 users and 39 real research runs over Harpenden's 1.1 GB corpus. **microclub/firefly** is a supervised zombie — no real traffic since May, and its post-mortem contains the sentence that is basically fm2's founding charter: *"my decision that the code produced (by 2025-era Claude Code) wasn't robust enough for me to support in the wild."*

## Five findings that should drive the design

**1. Identity is fragmented four ways.** You exist as "Ash Nehru" (fieldnote bearer tokens), "asnaroo" (muon login), "asnaroo" again (`~/.ftr-auth`), and firefly has a fourth email+device scheme — same phone number throughout. And your own decisions.md already worked out the right shape: **membership is a distinct axis from capability** — they compose, they don't merge. For the Sevenoaks app the ring level is exactly that membership axis, so fm2's context object wants three orthogonal facts about a user: who they are, what ring they hold, what capabilities are enabled.

**2. The privacy story is a strong promise with fail-open enforcement.** The doorstep promise ("a recording becomes a transcript tagged to a street, never a person") is well designed — but anonymise is a cred-gated Claude call that *silently no-ops without an API key* (12 of 80 notes still hold raw transcripts), every note JSON stores the uploader's raw `ip`, metre-precision GPS, and the resolved `address`, and the raw audio — identifiable voices stating political opinions at identified doorsteps, the textbook Article 9 case — is retained indefinitely, unencrypted, with no per-person index for an erasure request. For a party-scrutinized app, fm2 must make anonymisation a **gate, not a stage** (nothing becomes visible until redaction succeeded), put a retention clock on raw media, and record consent. Your ring model helps here: raw capture can simply live at ring 0 ("self") until the pipeline earns its promotion.

**3. Offline is the requirement the lift dropped.** Legacy fieldnote had a working field-reality stack — IndexedDB queue, connection scoring (latency probe, `effectiveType`, `saveData`), 30-second background drain, keep-recording-while-uploading. The fm port deferred all of it, and 191 client-side "Load failed" errors are the field voting on how much it matters. Also telling: the app records 13–75 MB *video* webm for what is an audio product. fm2's capture path should be designed around the queue from day one, probably audio-first with chunked resumable upload.

**4. Ops failures were structural, not bad luck.** The three-week restart loop (`localhost`→`::1` vs IPv4-only binds, ~8,400 failed Claude escalations, forced reboot on an 8 GB box), the Postgres that no supervisor watched while the *app* self-healed its own database, the watchdog that broke silently in a rename and mailed errors for four months, launchd unable to exec paths containing `ø`, dev and prod sharing `$HOME` context files, six hand-run backfill scripts because pipeline stages weren't resumable. For a campaign-team server with a support person who isn't you, each of these becomes a design input: supervise *dependencies* not ports, resumable-by-construction pipelines, immutable releases, boring paths.

**5. The integration thesis was already discovered.** The lift's method.md contains the best design idea in the whole archive: every tool composes four surfaces — **see, act, ask, move** — and the anatomy is diagnostic. fieldnote lacks *ask* (you can record but not query the transcripts); daylight lacks *move* (you can ask but not browse); and *fieldnote's missing ask is daylight's ask over a different corpus*. A canvasser asking "what have people on this street said about bins, and what did the council actually decide?" is one question across both indexes — they even already share an embedding model. Add the geographic spine (county → constituency → ward → street, with the postcodes.io/Nominatim/ONS stack already built) as the tree that *move* navigates, and the unified app almost designs itself: **a post database on a geographic tree, with ring-gated visibility, four surfaces, and pipelines as promotions.**

All of this is saved to memory, along with the key remote paths (`experiments/fieldnote/spec/method.md` and `spec/decisions.md` are the two documents I'd treat as canon).

So — back to where you were about to take us: which fm1 design decisions do you want to change? My guess-list from before still stands (regex→AST, the symlink product mirror, `@after`-by-default, three parallel generated `g.*` files, live-tree serving), but you clearly have specific ones in mind, and with the app picture now on the table I'm ready to argue about them properly.

> OK: so my learnings have been as follows. 1) a weakness of fm1 is that it's impossible to tell which text is human/user-written, and which is agent-written. ftr/features/ solves this by grounding things in the conversation. 2) the literate code decision in fm1 is questionable: the agent tends to write prose that's too complex for laypeople to read and understand, and that's a general problem: the reader who wants to understand something has to track through the markdown, even if it's written at the wrong level for their understanding. A better solution is to keep agent-facing contextual data (like ftr/features does) and answer user questions by creating ad-hoc tutorials / guides / lessons / q&a sessions that automatically conform to the user's level. That in turn lets the code be "just code" and removes complexity in the tooling - we can get it down to just a smart linker that reads @after/@before comments in normal code, with a "one object per feature" pattern compiling directly. 3) working in low/no internet situations is mandatory, so we have to build from that standpoint. 4) Let's use lots of rust/wasm to make sure things are efficient and performant - I'm no longer constrained by my own lack of familiarity with tools and languages.

Saved. Now here's why I think these four decisions are stronger together than separately — each one fixes a problem another one creates.

## How the pillars interlock

**One-object-per-feature makes provenance nearly free.** ftr's most elaborate machinery — subtree hashes, anchor healing, the three-way staleness check — exists because feature nodes point at *line ranges inside a monolith*, which drift constantly. If the code itself is carved one object per feature, the ref from a feature node to its code is just a symbol: `capture::Capture`. It can't drift; it can only be deleted or renamed, both of which the linker sees. Most of ftr's staleness apparatus evaporates, and what survives is the valuable part: verbatim requests, conversation anchors, rules, never-built, deprecations. The feature tree and the linker share one identity space — the tree node *is* the documentation of the code object, and the linker can enforce the correspondence both ways (an object with no node, or a node with no object, is a build warning).

**Dropping literate code is what makes the linker smart-but-small.** fm1's build complexity — extract, transform-in-place, linemap, frozen bootstrap, byte-exact round-trips — was mostly the cost of markdown being the source of truth. With code as just code, rust-analyzer, rustfmt, clippy, and every agent tool work natively; the linker's only jobs are: parse `// @after note_captured`-style directive comments (tree-sitter makes this AST-real, not regex — fm1's acknowledged constraint, broken at last), check them (does the host exist? is the ordering sound? is an `@replace` colliding?), and emit the dispatcher as plain generated Rust — fm1's `G`, but compiler-checked and tree-shaken by `cargo` itself rather than by convention. Static-disabled features aren't in the binary because the generated dispatcher never references them; the security property comes from the linker, and the *verification* of it from the compiler.

**Rust/wasm is what makes offline-first honest.** The deep reason fm1 never built "roles" (client:/server:/anywhere:) is that client and server were different languages with different runtimes, so crossing the boundary always meant a generated seam. One Rust core compiled twice — wasm in the PWA, native on the server — dissolves the seam for everything that isn't inherently one-sided: the post model, the ring/visibility calculus, validation, the queue, media chunking, even the embedding search (bge-small runs fine in wasm or behind it). The client isn't a "thin renderer talking to the API"; it's *the same feature objects* running against a local store that syncs. Offline stops being a queue bolted onto an online app — the legacy fieldnote pattern, good as it was — and becomes the default execution mode: **every app is offline; the server is just the peer you sync with when you can.**

**And offline-first gives the rings teeth.** If the substrate is a local store + sync, then ring visibility is naturally a *sync scope*: a post at "close team" simply never syncs to a device whose holder is "activist". Enforcement lives in the sync layer server-side ("the server resolves, the server enforces" survives from fm1), not in UI filtering — which is exactly the auditable, party-defensible shape: one choke point, one log. Promotion becomes a recorded, quorum-signed event in the same log as everything else — which is also your GDPR audit trail for free.

## The architecture this implies

- **Server**: one Rust binary (axum or similar) + embedded SQLite (+sqlite-vec) + a media blob store keyed by content hash. No Postgres to supervise, no venvs, no PATH traps — the support person manages a systemd unit and a backup script. Slow AI work (Speechmatics, Claude anonymise/report) runs as a resumable job queue *inside* the same binary, journaled in SQLite, so backfill-by-hand-script is structurally extinct.
- **Client**: PWA (your own conclusion from the field: instant iteration beats TestFlight), thin JS/DOM shell over the wasm core; capture and queue built on the local store from day one.
- **The linker (`fm2` the tool)**: tree-sitter over normal Rust (comments keep it language-neutral for a future TS/zero backend), feature = module with one object, directives checked against the tree, dispatcher + product manifest emitted as code, provenance cross-checked. Small enough to be boring; smart where it counts.
- **The feature tree**: ftr's format, simplified by symbol-refs, maintained by the session hook + extraction pipeline — with the generated-tutorial surface ("explain this to a campaign volunteer / to the support person / to me") as the *human* face, replacing literate prose. That surface is also method.md's missing **ask**, aimed at the system itself.

## Three tensions to settle (with my recommendations)

1. **Directive comments vs Rust attributes.** Comments are language-neutral and keep the linker one tool; real `#[fm::after(note_captured)]` proc-macros would give IDE navigation and compile-time errors but marry the mechanism to Rust. I'd start with comments + a linker that fails loudly — you can add a sugar macro later without changing the model.
2. **Sync model.** Full CRDT is overkill: posts are append-only, promotions are monotonic, and the only genuinely concurrent edits are things like reactions/comments. An append-only event log per device with server-assigned ordering (and rings as sync filters) covers the campaign app; I'd resist anything fancier until a real feature demands it.
3. **September 1 vs the rewrite.** Doable *if* the prototype slice is: login (port the muon/auth-gate flow), post capture (audio/photo/text, geotagged, local queue), ring-scoped feed + map, promotion flow — with the AI pipeline stages stubbed as jobs that can land in week 3 or after. The linker itself starts embarrassingly small (parse, check, emit one dispatcher) and grows under the app, exactly how fm1's build grew under muon — but this time the app is the point.

The one thing I'd add to your four, drawn from the archaeology: **make the privacy invariants linker-checkable from day one** — anonymise-before-visibility, no raw `ip`/address on ring>0 records, retention clock on raw media. fm1 proved conventions enforced by the build (the glossary!) actually hold; these are the conventions the party reviewers will ask about.

Where do you want to drill first — the linker's directive semantics (the `@on`-inversion question is still live), the post/sync data model, or the Sept-1 slice?

## What earned its keep (port unchanged)

- **Problem-before-mechanism.** The best sentence pattern in the tree: *"a singer often starts before the bar line, so cutting exactly on the downbeat chops the first syllable; a loop therefore carries `pre`."* Every mechanism arrives as the answer to a stated need. This is what transfers *intent*, which is the whole point of agent-facing context.
- **One worked example with real numbers threaded through** (the MJ track at 119.268 BPM, anchor 0.2182 s). Concreteness is what keeps prose honest.
- **Scoping at the least common ancestor + never restate an ancestor.** Prevents duplication rot; makes each node's job small.
- **The banned-phrase list** ("the magic happens", "load-bearing", summarizing final paragraphs). Negative rules are crude but this one visibly worked — I found no burble in the sampled nodes.
- **Honesty beats coverage**, rules as present-tense testable requirements, journeys as story. All keep.

## Where it falls short

**1. It serves two audiences and admits neither.** The rules say "plain-language, no jargon" — aimed at a lay reader — but `pre.md`'s actual prose is *"it returns the wrap points `[a − s, b − s)`, the unchanged `anchor`, and `lead`"*: precise, dense, and impenetrable to a layperson. That's not a failure of discipline; it's the correct register for the actual reader (the next agent, and you), colliding with a rule written for a reader who doesn't visit. ftr never resolved this because its tree doubles as public documentation. **fm2 should commit: the tree is written for the next agent.** Precision beats accessibility; jargon is fine *once defined at the right ancestor*; the lay reader is served by the explanation surface (decision 2), which generates tutorials *from* these nodes and demos at whatever level the reader needs. One artifact, one register, and the human-facing register becomes a rendering, not an authoring constraint.

**2. The style lives in an exemplar, not in the rules.** "Match `loop.md`" doesn't port to a new repo with no loop.md. The rules should carry the style: I'd distill the exemplar's actual moves into named requirements — *open with the problem; one concept per paragraph; thread one real example through; every subsystem node ends by naming its children's jobs in one clause each* — plus a short embedded exemplar in the skill itself.

**3. No length budget.** Quality rules but no size rules, and prose expands to fill agent enthusiasm. Proposal: budget by role — a subsystem node gets the 3–6 sentence model plus its vocabulary paragraphs; a leaf gets its delta, typically one paragraph; a bugfix gets *what was actually wrong and where the fix lives*, which `pre.md` does beautifully in two paragraphs ("The reported failure was not in that path" is the most valuable sentence in the file).

**4. Prose doing structure's job.** `pre.md` ends with a hand-written paragraph enumerating its children with links — that's `.order.md` rendered by hand, and it will drift when children change. In fm2 the viewer should render child navigation from `.order.md`, and the style rules should ban prose child-listings.

**5. Agent prose has no provenance.** Pillar 1 marks *user* text, but implementation sections don't record when they were written or against which code state. Cheap fix, consistent with the constitution: stamp each implementation section with its own ctx anchor (session + ts). Then "this prose is older than the code it describes" becomes machine-detectable — the prose equivalent of the staleness check.

**6. Rules and demos should be one system.** ftr's `## rule` sections are "the testable spec" — but nothing tests them. In fm2, a rule should cite the demo that enforces it, and the linker's completeness check can flag rules with no demo: *a rule without a demo is an aspiration, and should say so.* This is the demo pillar reaching into the prose style.

**7. No vocabulary enforcement.** fm1's machine-checked glossary (retired terms fail the build) demonstrably kept prose coherent across 43 specs; ftr's skill has nothing. fm2 should carry a `glossary.md` from day one with the same ratchet — cheap now, impossible to retrofit later.
