> # Building a Custom Rust Sync Engine for a PWA — Research Report (Aug 2026)
> 
> ## 0. Cross-cutting conclusion
> 
> The field has converged: for a single authoritative server, **you do not need CRDTs, OT, or vector clocks**. Figma, Linear, and Replicache/Zero all use the same shape — client outbox of named mutations, server-assigned total order via one monotonic version, delta pull, speculative local apply with rebase on server state. ElectricSQL's abandonment of CRDTs for a server read-path engine is further evidence. Your plan (append-only log, server as single choke point, SQLite both sides) is squarely on the well-trodden path; the ecosystem's verdict is also that you should **hand-roll the substrate** — the Rust event-sourcing framework space is a graveyard, and the primitives (rusqlite, axum SSE, prost, chacha20poly1305) are excellent.
> 
> ## 1. The server-authoritative op-log/rebase pattern
> 
> **Canonical component list** (all three systems agree): (1) client outbox of named mutations with per-client sequential mutation IDs, persisted locally; (2) server log with a single monotonic global version (Linear's `lastSyncId`, Replicache's cookie); (3) delta pull keyed by that version, realtime channel carrying either deltas (Linear) or a contentless "poke → pull now" hint (Replicache — simpler to make correct since all state flows through one pull path); (4) speculative apply in memory, rebase pending mutations over each incoming server state; (5) per-client `lastMutationID` high-water mark for exactly-once.
> 
> **Most copyable single decision — Linear's store discipline**: the durable client store holds *server-confirmed data only*; the outbox is a separate table; optimistic state lives only in memory; a transaction completes only when its delta arrives. This makes crash recovery, undo, and rebase tractable ([reverse-linear-sync-engine](https://github.com/wzhudev/reverse-linear-sync-engine), endorsed by Linear's CTO; [Artman talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bnOpm3a1fRE); [devtools.fm #61](https://www.devtools.fm/episode/61)).
> 
> **Replicache is the best-documented spec of the rebase mechanics** ([How Replicache Works](https://doc.replicache.dev/concepts/how-it-works)): server runs its own implementation of each mutator and its result is canonical (this is where validation/permissions live); on pull the client rewinds to the last server snapshot, applies the patch, drops mutations ≤ lastMutationID, replays the rest. **Figma** ([multiplayer blog](https://www.figma.com/blog/how-figmas-multiplayer-technology-works/)) shows the LWW-per-property variant and the anti-flicker rule (discard incoming server values for properties with unacked local edits); rebase-of-intent is the more general choice.
> 
> **Pitfalls checklist:**
> - **Idempotency**: dedupe by (clientID, mutationID); write the high-water mark *in the same transaction* as the mutation's effects, at snapshot isolation or better — SQLite's single-writer gives you this for free ([db-isolation-level](https://doc.replicache.dev/concepts/db-isolation-level)). Violating it produces double-applies and the "optimistic edit vanishes" flicker bug.
> - **Poison mutations**: a server-side mutator error must *advance the mutationID and record the error*, never retry forever — otherwise one bad mutation wedges the client's queue ([push guide](https://doc.replicache.dev/byob/remote-mutations)).
> - **Old clients**: mutations are a wire protocol. Version them (`schemaVersion` on push/pull), never delete a server handler, only add. Your single-Rust-server + shared wasm mutator code avoids the two-implementations-drift problem but not the versioning need.
> - **Ring-scoped sync is a solved shape**: Replicache's [Row Version strategy](https://doc.replicache.dev/strategies/row-version) (per-row versions + a per-client Client View Record, diffed on each pull) or Linear's sync-groups with membership changes delivered as sync actions. A naive per-ring log tail handles forward grants but you must explicitly design **retroactive grant** (backfill of rows the client couldn't see when logged) and **revocation** (synthetic deletes so the device actually forgets). CVRs are lossy-safe (lost CVR → reset patch).
> - Watch **Zero** ([custom mutators](https://zero.rocicorp.dev/docs/custom-mutators), [Zero 1.0](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/06/zero-version-1/)) for the field's direction: same rebase model, but the synced subset declared as queries rather than hand-written patch logic.
> 
> ## 2. SQLite in the browser, 2026
> 
> Mature and production-proven, with one correct configuration and several traps.
> 
> - **VFS choice**: official sqlite3 WASM **≥3.53** with **opfs-sahpool** — no COOP/COEP headers, works on Safari 16.4+, fastest official option; this is what **Notion ships** ([Notion wasm SQLite post](https://www.notion.com/blog/how-we-sped-up-notion-in-the-browser-with-wasm-sqlite)). Pin ≥3.50: 3.46.1/3.47 fixed a *corruption bug* in the SAB-based "opfs" VFS and 3.50 fixed a sahpool filename-digest bug ([sqlite persistence doc](https://sqlite.org/wasm/doc/trunk/persistence.md)). Alternative: **wa-sqlite OPFSCoopSyncVFS** (PowerSync's default; built-in multi-tab handoff, ~2–3x faster in benchmarks, holds up at 1GB+) ([PowerSync's May 2026 survey](https://powersync.com/blog/sqlite-persistence-on-the-web) is the best single reference). Avoid the COOP/COEP "opfs" VFS (breaks embeds/OAuth popups, corruption history). IndexedDB VFSes are fallback-only (Safari private browsing; degrades &gt;~100MB).
> - **Rust angle (new and important)**: **rusqlite 0.38 (Dec 2025) officially supports wasm32-unknown-unknown** via [sqlite-wasm-rs](https://github.com/Spxg/sqlite-wasm-rs), which ships an opfs-sahpool VFS port. Same rusqlite API on server and client is now realistic.
> - **Multi-tab**: OPFS sync handles are exclusive per file and unavailable in SharedWorkers, so the DB lives in one dedicated Worker with **single-writer leader election via Web Locks** (Notion's SharedWorker-router pattern if you need cross-tab queries; before adopting it Notion saw real corruption from concurrent tabs). Hold a Web Lock to prevent background-tab suspension.
> - **iOS/Safari eviction**: Safari's 7-day ITP storage deletion **does not apply to installed home-screen web apps** ([WebKit storage policy](https://webkit.org/blog/14403/updates-to-storage-policy/)) — push users to install. Call `navigator.storage.persist()` early (Safari 17+ honors it, especially for installed apps); quotas are now generous (~60% of disk per origin on Safari 17+).
> - **The strategic simplification**: because your substrate is an append-only log replicated from the server, **treat the local DB as a disposable materialized cache** — keep the last-acked cursor, run `PRAGMA integrity_check` on open, and nuke-and-resync on corruption or eviction rather than repair. This dissolves most of the browser-storage risk.
> 
> ## 3. Rust crates
> 
> - **CRDTs: skip for structured data** (see §0). If you later add collaborative text, embed one per text field (the Linear pattern): **loro** is the top pick (stable 1.x, fastest, shallow snapshots cap history growth — [loro.dev](https://loro.dev/)); **automerge** (3.0 fixed memory blowup) and **yrs** are credible; avoid diamond-types and cola as dependencies.
> - **Event-sourcing frameworks: hand-roll.** thalo unmaintained; eventually/eventsourced dormant; disintegrate active but Postgres-only; only cqrs-es + barely-used sqlite-es supports SQLite ([cqrs](https://github.com/serverlesstechnology/cqrs)). An `events(stream, seq, type, payload)` table with `UNIQUE(stream, seq)` optimistic concurrency is ~200 lines.
> - **SQLite**: **rusqlite both sides**. Server: WAL mode, one dedicated writer connection/task + read pool — pooled writers wreck SQLite write performance ([writeup](https://emschwartz.me/psa-your-sqlite-connection-pool-might-be-ruining-your-write-performance/)). Avoid sqlx-for-sqlite ceremony; **turso** (Rust SQLite rewrite) is explicitly beta — not yet.
> - **Delta push**: **axum SSE over WebSocket** for one-directional deltas — browser auto-reconnect + `Last-Event-ID` gives you cursor resume for free; on `broadcast::RecvError::Lagged`, drop the client into catch-up-from-log rather than replaying the channel ([axum #1670](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum/discussions/1670)); `Sse::keep_alive` for proxies. WS only if you need low-latency upstream ops on the same pipe.
> - **Serialization**: **bincode is dead** ([RUSTSEC-2025-0141](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2025-0141.html)). Use a versioned envelope `(schema_version, event_type, payload BLOB)` with **prost/protobuf for the durable log** (field tags, unknown-field tolerance = schema evolution); postcard acceptable only for ephemeral frames where both ends deploy together.
> - **Study, don't adopt**: PowerSync's Rust sync core (bucket/checkpoint architecture), LiveStore (the closest published analogue to your whole design: event log as source of truth, materialized into SQLite, git-style pull/rebase — [docs](https://docs.livestore.dev/evaluation/how-livestore-works/)). Avoid cr-sqlite (stalled) and sqlsync/Graft (alpha).
> 
> ## 4. Encryption at rest, per-ring keys, GDPR erasure
> 
> **Key framing**: in a server-trusted model, encryption cannot enforce ring visibility (the server holds all keys) — rings remain application logic at the choke point. Encryption addresses stolen disks/backups and, crucially, **GDPR erasure**.
> 
> - **Proportionate stack**: server FDE as hygiene + **application-level envelope encryption**: **one DEK per data subject** (not per event), XChaCha20-Poly1305 ([RustCrypto chacha20poly1305](https://cryptography.rs/)), DEKs wrapped by a KEK held outside the DB. Split every event into a non-personal envelope (id, type, ring, timestamps, causal refs — so replay still works after shredding) and an encrypted personal payload.
> - **MLS (RFC 9420) is the wrong trust model** — its entire cost (TreeKEM, epochs, credential infra) buys confidentiality *against the server* ([RFC 9750](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9750.html)), which you don't want. Per-ring keys with rotation on membership change are mostly theater when clients receive plaintext over TLS anyway; if you want the option (ring-scoped shredding, future E2E path), a ring-id+epoch wrapped-key table is ~50 lines. [OpenMLS](https://github.com/openmls/openmls) exists if requirements ever flip to E2E.
> - **Crypto-shredding is regulator-endorsed as of 2026**: EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 (blockchain, v2.0 adopted July 2026) explicitly accept key destruction as effective erasure ([Bird &amp; Bird summary](https://www.twobirds.com/en/insights/2026/netherlands/edpb-adopts-final-guidelines-on-blockchain-and-personal-data-a-practical-guide-for-organisations), [PDF](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2026-07/edpb_guidelines_202502_blockchain_v2_en.pdf)). Erasure = delete DEK + audit record + erasure event that every projection handles (purge read-model rows), + search-index rebuild, + blob deletion. The pattern's biggest payoff is **backups**: if backups only ever contain ciphertext and keys live separately, key deletion erases across all backups at once. Canonical write-ups: [Verraes](https://verraes.net/2019/05/eventsourcing-patterns-throw-away-the-key/), [event-driven.io](https://event-driven.io/en/gdpr_in_event_driven_architecture/).
> - **Pitfalls**: media blobs (a photo *of* someone is their data even in another's post — encrypt per subject or hard-delete), FTS indexes storing plaintext tokens, SQLite WAL/temp files, server logs. Unlike Kafka, SQLite lets you also **hard-delete shredded ciphertext later** in a compaction pass — do both.
> - **Client-side at-rest is mostly theater** — any key the JS can use, an attacker with the OS profile can use; the SQLite team says so outright ([wasm SEE note](https://sqlite.org/wasm/doc/trunk/see.md)). The real lever: **don't sync special-category data to the replica at all**, or sync with short TTL and purge on logout. Session-derived key over the OPFS VFS is the one variant that adds value (theft while logged out).
> - **Retention**: written retention schedule; auto-expire subject DEKs after the retention period — turns policy into one enforcement point. Crates: chacha20poly1305, [age](https://docs.rs/age/latest/age/) for backups/blobs, [aws-lc-rs](https://github.com/aws/aws-lc-rs) if FIPS-ish; avoid tink-rust; don't take new direct deps on ring (maintenance concerns).
> 
> ## 5. Resumable media upload from flaky mobile
> 
> - **Don't adopt tus wholesale** — build a small **content-addressed chunk protocol** that matches your sync engine's idempotency philosophy: client copies bytes into OPFS at capture time (iOS `File` handles are transient re-transcoded temp files — copy immediately), computes BLAKE3 whole-file + per-chunk hashes in wasm, writes an `upload_intent` row into SQLite (unified outbox). Server: `GET /blob/{hash}` → chunk-set present; `PUT /blob/{hash}/{index}` with chunk-hash header, idempotent; assemble + verify + emit `media_available` event. Events reference media by content hash; serve with immutable cache headers. Scope dedupe per account (hash-probe leak). This is strictly stronger than tus's optional checksum extension. If you'd rather be spec-compatible: tus v1 via [fileloft-axum](https://lib.rs/crates/fileloft-axum) (young 0.x, but the only maintained embed-in-axum option; rustus is stalled since Mar 2024) + tus-js-client with a **custom fingerprint** (iOS re-transcodes picked media, breaking default fingerprints — [tus-js-client#142](https://github.com/tus/tus-js-client/issues/142)). The IETF successor (draft-ietf-httpbis-resumable-upload, draft-12 July 2026) is still not an RFC — mirror its offset-probe concept, don't wait for it.
> - **Chunk size 1–4 MB** (expected waste per failure ≈ failure_rate × chunk/2; stay under proxy caps like Cloudflare's 100 MB); 2–3 parallel PUTs, drop to 1 on failures.
> - **Background upload reality 2026**: Background Sync and Background Fetch remain **Chromium-only** ([caniuse](https://caniuse.com/background-sync)); iOS suspends JS ~7–30 s after backgrounding and aborts in-flight fetches with no workaround ([Apple forums](https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/777860)); `fetchLater()` is Chromium-only and beacon-sized. So: **foreground-only uploads that survive being killed at any byte**, retry on `online`/`visibilitychange`/launch, Background Sync as Chromium-only enhancement, and — the best iOS lever — hold a **Screen Wake Lock** while draining the outbox (works in installed PWAs since iOS 18.4, [caniuse](https://caniuse.com/wake-lock)).
> 
> ## 6. Deterministic replay/testing — the minimal discipline
> 
> The full FoundationDB/TigerBeetle apparatus (single-threaded sim, simulated network/disk, seeded fault injection at 1000x speed — [Will Wilson talk notes](https://alex-ii.github.io/notes/2018/04/29/distributed_systems_with_deterministic_simulation.html), [VOPR doc](https://github.com/tigerbeetle/tigerbeetle/blob/main/docs/internals/vopr.md)) is overkill for one server + one client class, but the *rules* that make it possible are cheap and worth adopting from day one:
> 
> 1. **Determinize the core**: event application (log → state) must be a pure function. Inject `Clock` and `Rng` traits everywhere; timestamps and IDs (UUIDs!) are assigned by the server *and recorded in the event*, never regenerated at replay. All effects flow through the log.
> 2. **Kill the ambient nondeterminism**: no `HashMap` iteration order in anything that affects output (Rust's SipHash is randomly seeded — use `BTreeMap` or sort); no unordered `SELECT` feeding state (always `ORDER BY seq`); no SQLite `random()`/`CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` in logic; avoid float accumulation in state.
> 3. **Seeded property tests**: generate random op schedules (interleavings of client mutations, pulls, disconnects, ring-membership changes) from a single seed; print the seed on failure — seed + commit reproduces the bug exactly, the core FDB/TigerBeetle payoff.
> 4. **Replay oracles**: after replay, compare a **state checksum** (hash over canonically-serialized tables) against the live run — TigerBeetle checks replica data files are byte-identical; your version is one function. Keep **golden logs** checked in for demos and regression (replay must reproduce byte-identical state across releases — this forces the mutation-versioning discipline of §1 anyway).
> 5. **Async layer**: run tests on Tokio's single-threaded runtime with `start_paused = true` (auto-advancing mock clock) and the seeded runtime RNG ([Tokio hidden gems](https://pierrezemb.fr/posts/tokio-hidden-gems/)). If you later want network-fault simulation, **turmoil** + the libc-override tricks of **mad-turmoil** is the current best practice ([S2's DST write-up](https://s2.dev/blog/dst) is the practical recipe: single thread, paused clock, override `getrandom`/`clock_gettime`, meta-test that two runs of the same seed produce identical trace logs). madsim is the heavier alternative (RisingWave uses it); **shuttle** (randomized scheduling, scales) vs **loom** (exhaustive, tiny cases only) are for concurrency primitives you probably won't hand-write ([shuttle docs](https://docs.rs/shuttle)); Antithesis is the hosted option if this ever matters commercially.
> 
> The deterministic-replay requirement and the crypto-shredding requirement interact once: replay after shredding must still work — which the envelope/payload event split in §4 guarantees (structure replays; shredded content renders as tombstones).</result>

The Rust/patterns researcher is back (the landscape survey and the feature-tree port are still running). Headline findings — and they're gratifyingly aligned with our prior:

- **The field has converged on exactly the shape we suspected**: for a single authoritative server, no CRDTs — client outbox of named mutations, server-assigned total order via one monotonic version, delta pull, speculative local apply with rebase. Figma, Linear, and Replicache/Zero all use it; even ElectricSQL abandoned CRDTs. The verdict is also to **hand-roll the substrate** — the Rust event-sourcing framework space is a graveyard, but the primitives (rusqlite, axum SSE, prost, chacha20poly1305) are excellent, and the core log is ~200 lines.
- **Ring-scoped sync is a solved shape** — Replicache's "row version" strategy (per-client view record, diffed each pull) handles it, with two cases we must design explicitly: retroactive grant (backfill after promotion) and revocation (synthetic deletes so a device actually forgets).
- **SQLite-in-browser is production-proven** (Notion ships it): official wasm SQLite ≥3.53 with opfs-sahpool, DB in one dedicated worker with Web Locks leader election — and rusqlite 0.38 now officially supports wasm, so *the same Rust storage code genuinely runs both sides*. Strategic simplification: the client DB is a disposable materialized cache — nuke-and-resync on corruption rather than repair.
- **GDPR erasure has a regulator-endorsed answer as of July 2026**: crypto-shredding (EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 explicitly accept key destruction as erasure). Pattern: one data-encryption key per *subject*, events split into non-personal envelope + encrypted payload, erasure = delete the key — which erases across all backups at once. Replay still works; shredded content renders as tombstones. This is the clean answer to "append-only log vs right to erasure."
- **Media**: don't adopt tus — a small content-addressed chunk protocol (BLAKE3 hashes, idempotent chunk PUTs, 1–4 MB chunks) matches our idempotency model and is stronger than tus's optional checksums. iOS still can't background-upload; the practical levers are uploads that survive being killed at any byte, retry on visibility/online events, and a Screen Wake Lock while draining (works in installed PWAs since iOS 18.4).
- **Determinism discipline** (for the demo pillar): inject Clock and Rng everywhere, server assigns IDs/timestamps *recorded in events*, no HashMap iteration order in state, seeded property tests that print their seed, golden logs checked in, state checksums as replay oracles. The full TigerBeetle apparatus is overkill; these rules from day one are cheap.

> # State of local-first sync engines, August 2026
> 
> ## The headline
> 
> Between 2024 and 2026 the field split in two. **Server-authoritative sync engines won** for apps with one authoritative server: optimistic client mutations rebased against a server-ordered log ("server reconciliation"), plus query-scoped partial replication. **CRDTs retreated** to collaborative text/documents and genuinely decentralized/E2EE settings. The consolidation wave confirms it: ElectricSQL → Databricks (Aug 11, 2026; Electric Cloud discontinued, OSS continues at electric.ax), Triplit → Supabase (Oct 2025), Neon → Databricks, y-sweet's Jamsocket → Modal, Replicache archived/Reflect shut down in favor of Zero, cr-sqlite dormant (its author now at Rocicorp), and Jazz 2.0 (Apr 2026) pivoted from cryptographic CRDTs to a trusted server with row-level security — "users valued the feel, not the cryptography."
> 
> ## Tool survey (compressed)
> 
> | Engine | Model | Storage | Partial sync / permissions | Rust/wasm | Maturity / license |
> |---|---|---|---|---|---|
> | **Automerge** | op-based CRDT, full history DAG | columnar binary ("Hexane"); IndexedDB adapters | doc-granularity; no stock auth; Keyhive/Beelay = pre-alpha answer | Rust core; `samod` Rust repo | GoodNotes, Bowtie; MIT; 3.0 (Jul 2025) cut memory &gt;10x |
> | **Yjs/yrs** | delta-state YATA CRDT | agnostic (y-indexeddb; provider-side) | per-doc at provider (Hocuspocus/y-sweet/Liveblocks — server now AGPL OSS) | `yrs` mature Rust port | most-deployed collab engine; MIT; one-maintainer risk |
> | **Loro** | Eg-walker op-log CRDT | app-supplied | per-room auth hooks in Loro Protocol (Rust server) | Rust core + wasm + pure-TS | active, small team, MIT, no SaaS |
> | **Jazz 2.0** | git-like snapshot DAG (ex-CRDT) | Rust core, RocksDB server | trusted-server RLS via TS policy queries + JWT; E2EE opt-in per column | Rust core, wasm | alpha; MIT + Jazz Cloud |
> | **Evolu** | encrypted column-LWW event log, RBSR sync | SQLite everywhere (OPFS wasm) | zero-knowledge relay; **no server policy by design** | pure TS | solo-maintained, MIT incl. relay |

> | **Replicache/Reflect** | mutation rebase (the origin) | — | — | — | archived 2026 / retired 2024 → Zero |

> Risers: **TanStack DB** (the common client layer over Electric/PowerSync/REST), **Convex** (Rust backend, FSL, reactive server-authoritative), Cloudflare Durable Objects as sync substrate, PGlite (10M+ weekly downloads), Keyhive/Beelay.
> 
> ## Synthesis answers
> 
> **1. CRDT vs server-authoritative.** Settled: with one server, use it. Linear (transactions execute only on the server; monotonic `lastSyncId` total order), Figma ("since Figma is centralized, we can simplify" — per-property LWW, no CRDTs), and Zero/Replicache (optimistic mutators replayed authoritatively, git-style rebase) are the reference designs; Weidner's server-architectures essay is the theory ("literal CRDTs are often overkill in a central server app" — but design ops CRDT-*ishly*: idempotent, rebase-friendly). The killer argument: CRDTs resolve data-structure conflicts, not business conflicts (Convex's "A Map of Sync"; Cinapse publicly migrated off CRDTs to PowerSync, Oct 2025). CRDTs remain right as an embedded *field type* for rich text (yrs/Loro/Automerge) and for P2P/E2EE.
> 
> **2. Permission-scoped partial replication.** Converged best practice: **read scope = a named, server-evaluated query in real code, with identity injected server-side.** Zero's synced queries are the design north star (client calls a named query; your server injects `ctx.userID` and returns permission-filtered ZQL — the DSL approach was deprecated); PowerSync buckets are the proven scalable enforcement (JWT-claim parameter queries; buckets shared across users solves fan-out; pitfalls: full reprocess on rule changes, ~1,000 buckets/user); Electric's gatekeeper is the minimal version (proxy sets the WHERE; single-table filters force denormalized `tenant_id`; no auto-revocation mid-sync). Universal rules: align replication unit with permission unit; trust only server-derived identity; denormalize auth keys; enforce writes separately from reads.
> 
> **3. Offline blob upload.** Metadata in the sync log, bytes out-of-band — unanimous (PowerSync attachments is the published blueprint). Protocol: **tus 1.0** now; the IETF resumable-upload draft (-12, not yet RFC, Apple ships it natively) is a mechanical migration later. Browser: Background Fetch is still Chromium-only — no iOS — so use a foreground chunked-upload queue; record incrementally into **OPFS** (3–4x faster than IndexedDB for media) with `navigator.storage.persist()` + installed PWA. Content-address blobs (BLAKE3 hash keys) for idempotent retries, integrity, dedup.
> 
> **4. Event sourcing substrate.** Still sound — arguably best-in-class for a new, single-team, low-collaboration local-first app (LiveStore's whole thesis; client migrations become "drop the read model and replay"). Non-negotiable mitigations: weak-schema events + upcasters from day one (Greg Young/Dudycz), intent-named domain events only, per-scope log segmentation, snapshotting + compaction plan, and blobs/PII never in the log. Prefer state sync when a server DB already owns truth or fan-in is high.
> 
> **5. GDPR + immutable logs.** EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 explicitly bless **crypto-erasure** (destroy the key = erased). Ranked patterns: (1) keep PII/media out of the log — events carry hashes and subject IDs; erasure becomes a DELETE; (2) crypto-shredding with per-subject DEKs for PII that must ride in events; (3) `SubjectErased` tombstone + server compaction (Kafka's documented mechanism); (4) log rewriting as break-glass. Never put personal content in full-history CRDTs (Yjs/Automerge retain deleted content by design — "you can't delete Yjs documents").
> 
> ## Recommendation for your Rust-server + wasm-client PWA
> 
> All five answers point at one architecture: **server-authoritative event log (per-project/per-user, `lastSyncId`-ordered, client rebase) + content-addressed immutable blob store (BLAKE3, tus-resumable upload from an OPFS queue) + mutable PII vault with crypto-shredding.** Buy vs build: **PowerSync** is the best off-the-shelf Rust fit (Rust client core, alpha Rust SDK, backend-agnostic writes, FSL self-host, a decade in production); **Electric** the best plain-HTTP read path to front with a Rust proxy; **Zero** the best design to imitate but TS-only; **LiveStore** validates the event-sourcing pattern but is v0.4 TS — imitate, don't embed. Add yrs/Loro only if collaborative text appears. Watch: Zero post-1.0, Electric under Databricks, PowerSync Sync Streams, Graft, Keyhive, the RUfH RFC.
> 
> All claims carry primary-source citations in the published report (project docs, Linear/Figma engineering posts, Weidner/Convex essays, EDPB guidance, IETF datatracker).</result>

Both researchers are now home, and they agree with each other almost embarrassingly well — server-authoritative log with client rebase won the field, CRDTs retreated to collaborative text, scoped replication converged on server-evaluated queries, and the EDPB has blessed crypto-erasure. That's enough convergence to write the design. Drafting `sync.md` now.

`sync.md` is written and linked from fm2.md. The design in one paragraph: **server-reconciled optimistic mutation** — named, intent-carrying mutations applied speculatively client-side from a durable outbox, re-executed authoritatively by the server into an append-only log with one monotonic sequence; state on both sides is a materialized view of the log; one shared Rust mutator implementation compiled to wasm and native kills the drift problem. Scope enforcement is a server-evaluated query plus per-client view records, which uniformly handles normal flow, retroactive grant (promotion backfill), and revocation (synthetic deletes — the device genuinely forgets). Media goes out-of-band through a BLAKE3 content-addressed chunk store. Erasure is layered: personal content out of the log where possible, per-subject crypto-shredding where not (EDPB-blessed, backup-proof), retention as key expiry — and replay survives erasure because envelopes are never encrypted. The determinism section carries the demo pillar's demands: injected clock/entropy, server-assigned IDs recorded in events, seeded schedule tests, golden logs with state checksums.

Notable rejections, stated in the doc with reasons: CRDTs (the field's own retreat — business conflicts need an authority), E2E/MLS encryption (the server is the trust and enforcement point by design; per-ring crypto would be theater), frameworks (graveyard; primitives are excellent; PowerSync named as the fallback if hand-rolling stalls).

The parts most worth your argument:

1. **The client-DB-as-disposable-cache decision** — nuke-and-resync instead of repair. I'm confident it's right (it dissolves the whole browser-storage risk class), but it constrains bootstrap cost, which matters on a field device with a big history.
2. **"How mutations meet the linker"** (open question in the doc) — projections are naturally `@on`-shaped: unordered contributions folding the same event. The sync layer may be where the directive-vocabulary inversion gets its first real test, which would be a nice unification of the two designs.
3. **The scope model's vocabulary** — I kept rings entirely out; sync.md speaks only of "scopes = named server-evaluated queries." Check I didn't leak.

> My question: we're doing one object-per-feature, right? So wouldn't the cited code always live in the same folder as the node?

Yes — you've spotted the natural endpoint of decision 2, and it's worth making explicit because it changes the repo layout: **if a feature is one object, the folder is the feature.** The node, the code object, and the demo are the three faces sharing one name — so the honest filesystem layout is one folder holding all three:

```
features/fm2/notes/
  notes.md      ← the node (intent, verbatim requests)
  notes.rs      ← the code object (mechanism)
  demo.rs       ← the demo (behaviour)
```

Then "cited code lives in the same folder" isn't a convention the tooling checks — it's a tautology. The tree *is* the source tree, the viewer's cited-code section defaults to "show my sibling file," the PreToolUse hook's file→node lookup becomes `dirname`, and sharing/deleting/disabling a feature is a folder operation — which is the nøøb manifesto's "smallest shippable unit" made literal.

The mechanics are cheap on the Rust side: cargo doesn't care where source lives if the crate root points at it, and a generated `lib.rs` of `#[path = "../features/fm2/notes/notes.rs"] mod notes;` lines is exactly the kind of small, readable artifact the linker already emits (it's the dispatcher's sibling — the manifest made code). rust-analyzer handles `#[path]` fine. No extraction, no symlinks, no `imp/` — decision 2 survives intact; the linker just gains "emit the crate skeleton" as part of its job.

But line-range refs don't die entirely — three legitimate cases remain, all visible in today's tree and in ftr's best nodes:

1. **Cross-feature cites** — a subsystem node explaining its area cites its children's code; ftr's `loop.md` cites a dozen features. Under co-location these become rarer and mostly become `[links](#to/the/node)` instead of code refs — better anyway.
2. **Bugfix nodes** — ftr's `pre.md` is the exemplar: the complaint was about looping, the fix landed in `library.ts`. "The reported failure was not in that path" *requires* citing a path that isn't yours.
3. **Design-era nodes** — everything in the tree right now cites spans of `fm2.md`/`sync.md`, and those docs won't be carved into feature folders.

So my proposed formulation: **a feature's own code is implicit (the sibling file — no ref needed); an explicit ref is a signal that something crosses a boundary**, which makes refs *more* informative, not less. The staleness machinery shrinks to covering exactly the interesting cases.

One thing to decide before I write this into `fm2.md`: does the tree's *organizational* structure stay the same as the code's? The tree nests refinements and bugfixes as child folders (`prose-style/for-next-agent/`), and those children usually refine the *same* code object rather than owning a new one. ### p35
*2026-08-12 20:55*

> cool :-) shall we take the next step?

Next step it is: the **mutation/outbox layer with exactly-once semantics** — the last substrate piece the linker needs real material for. This makes the sync design's core promises executable: named mutations, client outbox, server-authoritative ordering, dedupe by (client, seq) in the same transaction as effects, poison mutations that record-and-advance instead of wedging, and client rebase. With a test that walks the whole offline→sync→rebase lifecycle deterministically.

Step complete — clippy-clean, all tests green. What now exists in `fm2-core`:

**`server.rs`** — the authoritative side. `Server::push` takes a mutation and a mutator closure (ultimately the dispatcher's job to route), and keeps the three promises from sync.md, each in one transaction: **exactly-once** (the per-client high-water mark commits atomically with the events, so a crash-retry is a clean `Duplicate`), **poison mutations record-and-advance** (a rejection stores the error and moves the mark — the queue can't wedge), and **in-order per client** (a `client_seq` gap returns `OutOfOrder` instead of silently swallowing a lost mutation).

**`outbox.rs`** — the client side, following Linear's store discipline: mutations journal durably before speculative apply, `pending()` is what a push drains and a rebase replays, and `ack()` deletes decided entries so crash recovery only ever resends the undecided tail. Confirmed state stays separate; optimistic state is memory only.

**`tests/sync.rs`** — the whole lifecycle as one deterministic story: three mutations captured offline (one of them the "unlucky 13" poison), speculative state predicted, push decides all three, a full crash-retry appends nothing, a gap is refused, then pull-and-rebase lands on the confirmed total. The test also demonstrates the design's quiet payoff: because client and server share *one* mutator implementation, the client's speculation already predicts the server's rejection — no flicker when the verdict arrives. That's the two-implementations-drift problem dead by construction.

The substrate skeleton is now: log + determinism kit + composition pattern + mutation lifecycle. The linker finally has everything it needs to formalize, so **linker v0 is the natural next step**: parse the `// @def` / `// @after` directive comments in the compose fixture with tree-sitter, check them, and regenerate the hand-written `g` module byte-identically — fm1's round-trip discipline as its first done-test. After that, the fixture features move into `features/` folders and the folder-is-the-feature layout goes live.

### p39
*2026-08-12 21:13*

> question: if we're writing code that's feature modular, don't we need to do the feature-tree mods before we start writing code?

Yes — and this is the point where the tree stops being documentation and becomes the front door of the workflow. You've caught an inversion we've been living with all day: we've been *folding* — code first, provenance after, a mirror maintained by subagents. That was the right shape for ftr, where the tree was mined from history. But under folder-is-the-feature, the node isn't a record *about* the code — it's the code's home. You literally cannot write a code feature without creating its folder, and the folder's first occupant is the node. So the order of operations flips by construction:

1. **Request arrives** → create the feature folder with its node: verbatim prompt, ctx anchor, title, purpose. This is now the act of *starting work*, not documenting it.
2. **Code object and demo** get written into that folder, beside the node.
3. **The implementation section** is still written *after* the code lands — it describes what was built, so it can't precede it. (Same split ftr had: insert nodes early, write implementations late.)
4. **The fold pass** shrinks to what it's actually good at: catching refinements and rule nodes from conversation, verifying node↔object correspondence, repairing refs — a sweeper, not the primary capture.

And the enforcement is mechanical, not disciplinary: the linker's completeness check already says *an object without a node is a lint error*. Once the layout is live, node-first isn't a rule anyone has to remember — code without a home simply doesn't build. It's also the strong version of ftr's hook philosophy: the hook pushed intent into context *before an edit*; this puts intent on disk *before the code exists*.

One honest caveat to build in: not every feature is specified before it's discovered — sometimes you find the feature by hacking. The rule accommodates that the same way demos do: create the node the moment the thing gets a name, even with a stub purpose, and the tree marks it incomplete until the faces fill in. What's banned isn't exploration; it's *homeless code*.

### p43
*2026-08-12 21:30*

> Just to test my understand of what feature modular means: when we create a new feature, we create a class representing that feature, and give it methods (static methods) that are decorated with // @ macros - they control how those are composed to create methods of the global object G, and call G's methods. Is that accurate?

Close — you've got the composition model right, but three details are worth sharpening, because they're exactly where fm2 differs from fm1. Using the real fixture as the example:

**1. It's an object with state, not a class of statics.** A feature's code face defines one struct, and that struct *is* the feature's state — `stats` owns `notes: u64, words: u64`. The directive-annotated methods are ordinary instance methods (`&mut self`), because a contribution usually reads and writes its own feature's data. In fm1 everything was function-poking with state elsewhere; in fm2 the object is the point — it's the "one object per feature" pattern, and it's what makes a feature a deletable, shippable unit.

**2. The directives describe contributions to *hosts*, and `g` is a generated module of functions — not a global object.** A host is just a named function that exists because some feature declared it with `// @def` (that feature is the *owner*). Other features attach to it with `// @after` / `// @before` / `// @replace`. The linker reads those comments and *generates* the dispatcher — plain Rust, one free function per host:

```rust
pub fn note_created(app: &mut App, id: u64, text: &str) {
    app.notes.note_created(id, text); // owner (@def)
    app.stats.note_created(id, text); // @after
}
```

The state that looks "global" isn't in `g` at all — it's in `App`, the *product's* struct, which has one field per composed feature. `g` is stateless routing; a different product (different manifest of features) gets a different generated `g` and a different `App`, over the same untouched feature code.

**3. Nothing is dynamic and there are no macros.** The `// @` things are plain comments; the linker parses them with tree-sitter at build time and writes ordinary code that the Rust compiler then checks and tree-shakes. That's deliberate: comments keep the mechanism language-neutral (the same linker can read TS or zero later), and generation-not-runtime is the lesson fm1 died learning (the global-scope poking that namespace clashes killed).

And your last clause is exactly right, with one emphasis: **anyone who wants the composed behaviour calls `g`'s function, never a feature's method directly.** Calling `app.stats.note_created(...)` yourself would bypass composition; only the generated dispatcher makes direct feature calls, in the order the linker determined. So the flow is: event or mutation arrives → `apply` calls `g::note_created(...)` → `g` fans out to owner then contributors. When a new feature wants to react to notes being created, it never touches `notes`'s code — it declares `// @after note_created` on its own object, and the linker regenerates `g` with one more line in it. That regenerated line *is* the feature being "added to the existing behaviour."

### p44
*2026-08-13 08:11*

> I'd make the last clause even stronger: it's *not possible* to call a feature method directly.

Agreed — and that's the difference between a pattern and an architecture: the pattern asks people to behave; the architecture makes misbehaving fail to build. In fm2 the enforcement is two-layered: outside the crate the *compiler* seals it (contribution methods are `pub(crate)`, so external code can't name them), and inside the crate the *linker* seals it — it already parses every feature file, so a direct call to a directive-annotated method from anywhere but the dispatcher becomes a build error. One nuance to keep: the seal covers *contribution methods* (directive-annotated). A feature's ordinary public API — `EventLog::append`, `Outbox::enqueue` — stays callable; that's the surface demos drive. What becomes impossible is invoking composed behaviour around the composition.
